items.title: Emergency, governor's rule imposed in KP as president approves cabinet decision
items.description: Key developments: Emergency imposed under Article 232 , governor’s rule under Article 234 Cabinet recommended move due to KP govt’s ‘ deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism’ Technocratic council formed ; Fakhr Alam appointed as KP chief secretary PTI’s Gohar condemns decision as undemocratic, says peace cannot be established by weakening provincial autonomy Governor Kundi calls for unity for ‘new chapter’ in KP’s development ISLAMABAD: The federal government on Sunday imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa following the president’s approval of the recommendations by the federal cabinet. The measures have been approved under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, the President House said in a statement. The two provisions pertain to the proclamation of emergency and governor’s rule. Following the imposition, internet disruptions were being reported from parts of Peshawar, with Dawn unable to contact its correspondents there. According to sources in the telecom sector, mobile network and data services have been slowed or shut down in selected areas of some cities. However, there is no province-wide shutdown of mobile data or internet. Internet watchdog NetBlocks said network data showed a major disruption to internet connectivity in parts of KP as emergency was imposed. The federal government also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in KP. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment. The decision to impose the emergency provisions came during an emergency meeting of the federal cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, where he was briefed on the security situation in KP. A statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said cabinet members reviewed the situation and took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. The members proposed, given the “gravity” of the situation, that the PM advise the president to exercise “his constitutional authority and impose an emergency in the province under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution”. The emergency imposition comes a day after PM Shehbaz met President Zardari and discussed the country’s overall security situation. That meeting came amid heightened tensions between the PML-N-led federal government and the KP government led by the PTI — which is in opposition in the Centre. They have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks . The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations. On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. It may be recalled that in July 2024, when Afridi’s predecessor Ali Amin Gandapur was the chief minister, the KP Assembly passed a resolution urging the federal government to consult with it and the provincial government before launching a new military operation. The resolution, passed by a majority vote, cautioned that proceeding without provincial consent could hinder the offensive’s success and result in adverse consequences, for which the federal government would be responsible. In December that year, the assembly voted unanimously against a potential military operation in parts of Khyber and Bannu districts. About a year later, after Afridi became the KP CM, the provincial assembly convened a grand jirga with Governor Faisal Karim Kundi and other parties in attendance. The moot unanimously demanded that the Centre prioritise negotiations with Afghanistan and consult the KP government over Afghan policy. Constitutional provisions Emergency Article 232 of the Constitution provides for the proclamation of emergency in a province. It says, “If the president is satisfied that a grave emergency exists in which the security of Pakistan, or any part thereof, is threatened by war or external aggression, or by internal disturbance beyond the power of a provincial government to control, he may issue a Proclamation of Emergency.” However, invoking this article “due to internal disturbances beyond the powers of a provincial government to control” requires a resolution from the provincial assembly of that province. In case the president “acts on his own” — which is not currently the case — the Proclamation of Emergency is to be placed before both houses of Parliament for approval by each house within 10 days. According to this provision, parliament “shall have power to make laws for a province, or any part thereof, with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Federal Legislative List” during the time of the proclamation of an emergency. Nothing in this Article shall restrict the power of a provincial assembly to make any law which the Constitution empowers it to make, but if any provision of a provincial law is repugnant to any provision of an Act by Parliament, the latter would prevail and the provincial law would be void as long as the parliamentary Act is in effect. Governor’s rule On the other hand, Article 234 deals with the imposition of the governor’s rule “in case of failure of constitutional machinery in a province”. For imposition of the governor’s rule, the president simply requires a request from the provincial governor, it says. “A proclamation issued under this Article shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months, unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolution of the joint sitting and may by like resolution be extended for a further period not exceeding two months at a time,” the Constitution reads. However, it adds that no such proclamation shall in any case remain in force for more than six months. Article 233, which provides powers to the president to suspend certain fundamental rights during the emergency period, was not mentioned in the summary signed by President Zardari. Where is Sohail Afridi? A couple of hours after the imposition of emergency was announced, KP Information Minister Shafi Jan, who had been accompanying now dysfunctional KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on the PTI’s long march , claimed that the he had been taken into custody. Dawn contacted police for a confirmation soon after Jan’s claim, but there was no response. Meanwhile, MNA Shahid Khattak also claimed Afridi’s “arrest”, as well as MNA Junaid Akbar and others from there party. He also said he would be leading the march now. Later, the PTI issued a statement, condemning the “arrest” of Afridi and other and describing it as an act of “political victimisation and an attempt to weaken the province’s elected leadership and democratic institutions”. It quoted PTI spokesperson Sheikh Waqas Akram as saying that Afridi’s “arrest” could not be viewed in isolation from the federal government’s decision to impose emergency and governor’s rule. “The developments reflect a broader effort to bypass elected institutions and undermine the constitutional authority of the province. “The arrest of Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and Junaid Akbar has exposed the political nature of the federal government’s actions. These measures are not directed at addressing security challenges; they are intended to weaken PTI, undermine the elected government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and disregard the democratic will of its people,” he said. Akram demanded the “immediate and unconditional release” Afridi, Akbar and “all other political detainees arrested in connection with the ongoing action against PTI”. He also demanded that the federal government publicly disclose the “legal grounds, specific charges and procedural basis for the arrests of the chief minister and the PTI provincial president”. However, he sounded less certain while speaking on Geo News programme ‘ Naya Pakistan ’. He said they had received reports of Afridi and Akbar’s arrest, and adding that they were unable to confirm whether Jan and Khattak, too, had been taken into custody. “We are unable to contact some people […] Because the internet has been suspended in several areas, we are unable to contact. You do not know the havoc they have created in KP. People are escaping and going into hiding,” he said. In a clip shared on PTI’s official X account, Salman Akram Raja, the party’s secretary general, said, “We do not know where Sohail Afridi is, in what condition he has been kept. Junaid Akbar is also missing.” When Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry was asked about reports of Afridi’s arrest during ‘ Naya Pakistan ’, he said some individuals had been detained in view of the law and order situation but did not confirm whether they included Afridi. He said those who did not have a criminal record or were not wanted would be released. Council, chief secretary appointed Following the imposition of emergency, the federal government formed an 11-member technocratic KP Advisory Council to assist the governor with running the province. Later, Governor Kundi also chaired the first meeting of the council, vowing to restore peace in the province. Earlier in the day, the federal government appointed Dr Muhammad Fakhr Alam Irfan as the chief secretary of KP, according to an official notification, a copy of which is available with Dawn. The appointment will take effect immediately and remain in place until further orders, it said. Dr Irfan, a Grade 22 officer of the Pakistan Administrative Service (PAS), was previously serving as secretary of the Power Division in the federal Ministry of Energy. He hails from Mardan. In a separate notification, the federal government also placed Muhammad Yahya Akhunzada at the disposal of the KP government with “immediate effect and until further orders”. Akhunzada, a Grade 20 PAS officer, was serving as an additional secretary at PMO. He hails from Charsadda and has also served as additional political agent for North and South Waziristan, secretary of health, information and education in KP, and commissioner of Dera Ismail Khan. ‘Peace cannot be established by weakening provincial autonomy’ PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan strongly condemned the imposition of emergency in KP and “completely rejected” it. “This is an extremely alarming and grave political mistake and an undemocratic measure — the people will never accept such actions against their rights,” Gohar wrote in a post on X. He stated: “There is still time; this decision can be withdrawn in a few days. Let the federation set aside its ego, understand the ground realities, accept legitimate demands, respect the sentiments and emotions of the people, and save the country from further political and economic damage and from pushing back the democratic process. “Revisiting political decisions is not a sign of weakness but of wisdom in the national interest — otherwise, great damage will be done.” Stressing that the mandate of the people of KP was their constitutional and legal right, the PTI chairman said: “Peace cannot be established, nor stability brought, by ignoring this mandate, weakening provincial autonomy, and creating conflict between the federation and the province.” He asserted that there was “no disagreement on eliminating terrorism, but the fight against terrorism cannot be used as a justification to suppress the people’s voice, achieve political objectives, or limit the province’s constitutional authority”. “Terrorism can only be combated through national unity and a joint strategy,” Gohar maintained. “The federation cannot be strengthened by weakening the provinces. The solution to problems lies not in force, confrontation, and extraordinary measures, but in political wisdom, supremacy of the Constitution, and meaningful negotiations and practical steps.” The PTI chairman said his party will raise the matter on “every constitutional, legal, and democratic forum for the protection of the people’s mandate, provincial autonomy, and constitutional and democratic rights”. Later in the day, Gohar said PTI would challenge governor’s rule through the courts, assemblies and public forums. The PTI parliamentary committee held a meeting and categorically rejected the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP. In a statement issued afterwards, it termed the development “a direct assault on the public mandate and an unacceptable move”. “In a three-hour-long meeting of the PTI parliamentary party, the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP was strongly condemned and unanimously rejected. The meeting declared this step contrary to facts, unconstitutional, undemocratic, and a blatant insult to the public mandate of the province,” the statement said. “The parliamentary party made it clear that measures to render the elected provincial government ineffective and usurp its constitutional powers could pose grave threats to the federal system and democratic traditions. Such decisions will increase political instability and public unrest in the province, while already existing tensions between the federation and the province will further intensify,” it added. The statement added that the solution to political differences should be found through constitutional and democratic procedures and mutual consultation, rather than through force and coercion. It also raised serious questions regarding the conduct of the federal government. “The parliamentary party took the stance that if terrorism and the deteriorating law and order situation are the primary justification for the imposition of emergency, then why is the situation in Balochistan being ignored?” the statement asked. The meeting also made it clear that Afridi was the elected chief minister and a member of the provincial assembly. “Measures regarding his arrest, detention, or the usurping of his constitutional and democratic powers were strongly condemned. The meeting termed such actions an insult to the public mandate and a dangerous precedent for democratic traditions,” it said. The Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP), of which PTI is a part, termed the move a violation of the Constitution. In a statement, the opposition alliance particularly assailed President Zardari’s PPP, claiming that the “most undemocratic actions and the imposition of governor’s rule” had been the hallmark of the party in the country’s history. “On the one hand, despite the extremely dire administrative and law and order situation in Balochistan, no such step has been taken, while on the other hand, this province — whose assembly and government stand on the true and real mandate of the people — has been targeted,” it contended. TTAP said it would convene a meeting on the matter and announce a joint course of action. Governor Kundi urges unity for ‘new chapter’ Meanwhile, Governor Kundi said the decision was made for “establishing peace in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the prosperity of its people, and the development of the province”. “I am your governor, but beyond that, I want to play my role as a servant of this soil and a protector of your rights. Let us come together to bring peace to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and begin a new chapter of our province’s development,” he said in a statement. Kundi assured the public that it was his responsibility to raise their issues on the relevant forums. Recalling the sacrifices made in the fight against terrorism, he said, “Now the time has come that we do not let these sacrifices go to waste and together establish lasting peace in our province.” The PPP leader urged the public to set aside their political differences and unite for the province’s peace, the protection of its people, and the future of the coming generations. “We must not let our differences become an obstacle in the path of our province’s common interests.” Cannot allow PTI to destabilise the economy: PM tells cabinet Addressing the cabinet meeting, the premier said the PTI-led KP government cannot be allowed to derail the stabilising economy amid tensions between the two sides. “I will not allow them (PTI) to destabilise the economy,” he said during the meeting. On terrorism in KP and Balochistan, the premier said, “The way common citizens are being martyred, the way police officials and security officials, children and mothers [..] there can be nothing more heart-wrenching.” He recalled that Pakistan has repeatedly urged neighbouring Afghanistan to rein in the terrorist elements; however, “they still do not understand it”. PM Shehbaz also reiterated his condemnation of the recent deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, noting the long-standing fraternal ties between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. “Our only goal is that peace should be restored in the region,” he said. “Pakistan expresses solidarity with Saudi Arabia and stands with it. We will not tolerate any aggression against Saudi Arabia,” he said, adding that it was a “red line” for Pakistan. During his address, PM Shehbaz also spoke of the recent staff-level agreement reached with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). “It is hoped that we will unlock the $1.2 billion tranche within this year,” he said, recalling a meeting with the IMF’s Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) last month. He commended the political and military leadership for “working together day and night” in bringing fiscal discipline to Pakistan. The premier recalled his visit to London last month, where he had met with senior executives from leading global financial institutions. He also spoke of Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts in the international community, taking note of the appreciation Pakistan has received for mediation in the Middle East conflict. “Pakistan continues to play its role with hard work and sincerity,” he said, particularly lauding the role of the Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir. Additional input by Ikram Junaidi, Kalbe Ali

items.title: « Re-Création 2026 » : : le DMWM forme près de 96 000 jeunes aux valeurs spirituelles et citoyennes
items.description: Le Dahiratoul Moustarchidina Wal Moustarchidaty (DMWM) a clôturé samedi 10 octobre, à Tivaouane, la quatrième édition de ses camps de vacances Re-Création. Pendant trois semaines, près de 96 000 jeunes ont reçu une formation spirituelle, morale et citoyenne, prolongée sur le terrain par de nombreuses actions au service des communautés. Les chiffres disent l’ampleur du rendez-vous. Pour sa quatrième édition, la Re-Création du Dahiratoul Moustarchidina Wal Moustarchidaty (DMWM) a réuni 95 838 pensionnaires, dont 11 542 sympathisants, répartis dans 670 daaras à travers le Sénégal. Le mouvement a aussi organisé des camps en Gambie, en Mauritanie et en Europe. La cérémonie nationale de clôture s’est tenue samedi 10 octobre dans la cité religieuse. Placée sous l’égide de Serigne Moustapha Sy Al Maktoum, l’édition s’est déroulée du 7 au 27 septembre sous la direction de Serigne Cheikh Ahmed Tidiane Sy Capitaine. Elle coïncidait avec la fin du premier semestre de Ràmmonte, le programme éducatif qu’il a lancé, et devait permettre de mesurer ce que les jeunes en avaient retenu. D’où le thème retenu, « Dund Ràmmonte », qui signifie vivre au quotidien les principes du programme. Le slogan, « N’est-il pas temps d’y associer les cœurs ? », s’inspire d’un verset coranique. Il invite à vivre l’acte de dévotion avec sincérité et conscience. Pendant 21 jours, les pensionnaires ont suivi huit modules complémentaires. L’étude du Coran et des hadiths devait les ramener aux principes fondateurs de l’islam, et la jurisprudence islamique leur a permis de réviser les fondamentaux de la charia. Les exercices comportementaux visaient à installer des habitudes saines, et le module de savoir-vivre en société à leur apprendre à exercer une influence positive sur leur entourage. Le « parcours des Héros du Ciel » leur a présenté des figures exemplaires, de Seydi Mouhamadoul Moustapha Sy aux gens de la caverne. Les classes de chant reposaient sur un poème de Serigne Cheikh Ahmed Tidiane Sy Al Maktoum, qui revisite les piliers de l’islam. Les activités sportives et les « activités utiles » complétaient le programme. Cette année, les organisateurs ont misé sur une pédagogie de l’application. Les cours, interactifs, étaient suivis d’exercices pratiques pour que les comportements enseignés en classe deviennent des habitudes. Sur le terrain, cette démarche a donné des résultats concrets. Les pensionnaires ont désherbé et nettoyé des établissements scolaires, des hôpitaux et des places publiques. Ils ont remis en état des tables-bancs, des portes, des fenêtres et des tableaux, construit des boxes d’hygiène et offert des fournitures scolaires aux écoles qui les accueillaient. Au total, 538 plants ont été mis en terre à travers le pays. La solidarité s’est aussi exercée hors des écoles. Des denrées alimentaires ont été offertes à des daaras, et des exemplaires du Coran ainsi que des vêtements ont été distribués. À Vélingara, la Maison d’arrêt et de correction a reçu seize ventilateurs. Lors de la cérémonie de clôture, le DMWM a remercié les inspecteurs et les directeurs d’école, dont la collaboration a permis d’accéder aux établissements. Dans son discours, Serigne Cheikh Ahmed Tidiane Sy Capitaine a exhorté les moustarchidines à poursuivre dans cette logique de quête spirituelle et d’engagement citoyen, bien au-delà des trois semaines de camp. Le mouvement entend ainsi faire de la Re-Création plus qu’une parenthèse de vacances : une étape dans la formation spirituelle, morale et citoyenne d’une jeunesse qu’il veut voir au service de la communauté. Cheikh Tidiane NDIAYE

items.title: 'No lesson learnt': KP emergency evokes grim October memories
items.description: Sunday, Oct 11, evoked grim memories for many in Pakistan, as the federal government imposed emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The cabinet was certain of the decision, but many others warned against repeating what they saw as an “ill-advised step”. Nevertheless, it happened, again. The threat of emergency and governor’s rule had been looming over the province for days, after the PTI announced its long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. It materialised on Sunday. It began with a federal cabinet meeting where Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was briefed on the security situation in KP, which the Centre had earlier been linking with the need for emergency in the province. The cabinet reviewed the situation, took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”, and gave the nod to impose emergency and governor’s rule in KP. A signature by President Asif Ali Zardari, and the decision was implemented shortly after. The development took veteran journalist Mazhar Abbas on a trip down memory lane, apparently a grim one. “Why [does] October often bring ‘bad news’ for democracy from 1958 to 2026?” he posted on X. “Saddest part is that each time one party or the other welcomed such moves. On Oct 12, 1999 when PM Nawaz was sacked, the PPP welcomed the move. Now, the PPP and PML-N agreed to get rid of the PTI KP government. No lesson learnt,” he lamented. Former ambassador and analyst Maleeha Lodhi agreed. “Really nothing learnt from history,” she too posted, replying to Abbas’s comment. Analyst Niaz Murtaza was more thorough in recounting the historical trend of what Abbas described as “bad news” from October. “October is perhaps the worst month for democracy,” Murtaza commented, sharing a list of instances from history: On the latest imposition of emergency in KP, he said the move was “deeply condemnable, unfortunate and ill-advised”. “The clearly illegitimate nature of the central government makes it doubly so. This could make the situation in KP much more complicated,” he warned. Others, too, warned against the move and its consequences. Among them was National Democratic Movement Chairperson Bushra Gohar, who posted a warning the night before emergency was imposed. “Emergency will further aggravate the already volatile political and security situation in Pakhtunkhwa. The province cannot afford yet another failed experiment after the disastrous pro-Taliban TTPTI government — 13 years of incompetence, loot and plunder, death and devastation,” she posted on X on the night before emergency was imposed. Instead, she added, free, fair and credible elections were the only way forward. Similarly, the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan cautioned the federal government and Parliament in a statement that declaring emergency or imposing governor’s rule in KP risked further deepening of political tensions and undermining of democratic processes. “We strongly urge the federal government and the PTI to resume a meaningful political dialogue immediately and ensure that citizens’ fundamental rights are not suspended under any pretext,” the statement said. Lawyer Rida Hosain said that by imposing emergency, the federal government has “undermined the democratic choice of the people of KP and its provincial autonomy”. “The authority of KP’s elected institutions flows from the people’s will, not from the dictates of the federal government,” she wrote on X. In another post, she pointed out that Article 175(3) of the Constitution had been deemed inapplicable for the duration of the emergency. “Article 175(3) mandates the separation of the judiciary from the executive. This paves the way for executive officers to perform judicial functions in these areas,” she explained. Similarly, journalist Munizae Jahangir termed emergency and governor’s rule a “spectacular failure of the politicians,the ruling party amd its allies”. They had set a “dangerous precedent and disenfranchised an entire province, while the opposition failed to negotiate a space for themselves where they could protect themselves and their citizens. The people of KP will now suffer the most,” she said. Lawyer Hassan Abdullah Niazi noted that throughout Pakistan’s history, the “imposition of an emergency has rarely resulted in better governance or democracy”. “We have normalised the extraordinary; the denial of fundamental rights,” he contended. He termed the decision “unconstitutional” and explained the reasons for his analysis in a series of posts on X. “Article 234 (governor’s rule) requires a demonstration that the constitutional machinery in a province has broken down. Nothing the government has said justifies this so far. The KP Assembly is working as is the cabinet,” Niazi explained. He went on to caution that “such a move will further fragment national stability” and “creates a dangerous precedent where the federation can simply dismiss troublesome provincial governments over political differences”. Senior journalist Zarrar Khuhro remarked, “While this has very little to do with terrorism, will emergency stop the bleeding. You guessed it: no.” Journalist Ihsanullah Tipu Mehsud saw emergency as a move that “frees the PTI” and “traps the Centre”. Because “Islamabad owns security, PTI owns the narrative”, he said on X. Former caretaker IT minister Umar Saif explained Mehsud’s deduction in more detail, saying that imposing emergency in KP “comes with an enormous burden of responsibility”. “It is not merely an exercise of authority; it is a commitment to fix what has gone wrong. The government must now deliver. Failure will deepen public disillusionment, hand fresh ammunition to the naysayers, and discredit the very idea of reform. “Reform demands clarity of intent, consistency of purpose, and the resolve to see it through. We have seen too many initiatives falter midway, leaving behind resentment and eroding faith in the process,” he said. Meanwhile, journalist Shahzad Iqbal noted that PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had called emergency a “political atomic bomb”. “Yet President Zardari has completed hat-trick of imposing governor’s rule,” he said, recounting the previous two instances — in 2009 in Punjab and in 2013 in Balochistan. “The irony is hard to miss,” he commented. Pakistan’s former ambassador to the United States Husain Haqqani also noted the repeated instances of emergency and governor’s rule in Pakistan, commenting: “What has happened repeatedly in the brief history of Pakistan does not happen in the long history of other countries.” Header image: A general view shows a road blocked with shipping containers amid ongoing protests by the PTI party demanding the release of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan in Peshawar on October 11, 2026. — AFP

items.title: ‘We must stick together’ — Haaland after Man City’s win amid financial charges
items.description: Erling Haaland said Manchester City’s 3-0 win at 10-man Liverpool showed they will “stick together” after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules. Haaland put City ahead at Anfield on Sunday before Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki netted to silence Anfield after Liverpool fans barraged them with taunts about the guilty verdict. Enzo Maresca’s side showed no signs of being fazed by the abuse in their first match since the club discovered an independent commission had found them guilty of breaking over 100 financial regulations. City, who are appealing against the decision, could face a massive points deduction that would likely lead to relegation or even be stripped of their titles. But for now Norway striker Haaland insisted their defiant performance at old rivals Liverpool proved they are still committed to the City cause. “Every single person that is part of Man City, and every fan, this is a lovely moment that will stay with us for a long time,” he said. “It was hard, but we showed amazing character from back to front. So proud of everyone. It’s always tough to come here. “Important to stay strong mentally, stick together and do what you can do something about and the thing we can do something about is to play good football and fight together. That’s the only thing we can do.” City were helped by Liverpool midfielder Ryan Gravenberch’s red card for two bookings just prior to Haaland’s opener. They ran riot after that to move three points clear at the top of the Premier League. Whether they are able to maintain a title challenge with a potential punishment looming remains to be seen. Haaland said City’s players can only concentrate on their performances while the club’s Abu Dhabi-based owners deal with the legal ramifications of the verdict. “You want to win games, it’s as simple as that. Perform well, play good football and win games. This was a mental battle,” he said. “Proud that we managed to stick together, we are mentally strong. Plenty of games coming up so time to recover and go again.” City midfielder Elliot Anderson delivered a composed display in his first taste of the rivalry with Liverpool after his close-season move from Nottingham Forest. The England international echoed Haaland’s assessment of his side’s spirit, saying: “Togetherness, fight, a tough place to come and we stuck together and fought for each other. We’ve showed courage. “The atmosphere was more than normal, arriving into Anfield and the first 10 minutes of the game. “We did well to quieten the crowd. Struggled first half but second we were better and then the goals came.” The post ‘We must stick together’ — Haaland after Man City’s win amid financial charges appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Rentrée scolaire 2026-2027 : le gouvernement mise sur une reprise progressive
items.description: Le ministre de l’Éducation nationale, Moustapha Mamba Guirassy, confirme la reprise des cours ce lundi 12 octobre 2026, malgré les difficultés persistantes dans certains établissements. Les 72 heures perdues devraient être rattrapées grâce à des ajustements de l’organisation scolaire. La rentrée scolaire est maintenue au lundi 12 octobre 2026 sur l’essentiel du territoire national, malgré les inondations qui affectent encore plusieurs établissements. Le ministre de l’Éducation nationale, Moustapha Mamba Guirassy, estime que l’évolution de la situation permet une reprise des cours, tout en reconnaissant que certaines écoles auront besoin d’un délai supplémentaire de 24 à 48 heures. Sur près de 30 000 établissements scolaires recensés au Sénégal, environ 644 avaient été initialement identifiés comme touchés par les inondations. Ce nombre est ensuite passé à un peu plus de 200, avant une nouvelle baisse à la veille de la rentrée. Le ministre n’a toutefois pas communiqué de bilan national définitif actualisé. Dans la banlieue dakaroise, les difficultés restent importantes. À Guédiawaye, 46 établissements publics sur 258 ont été affectés. En prenant en compte les structures publiques et privées, le ministre fait état de 1 374 établissements dans la zone, dont environ 3 % touchés. À Pikine, 62 établissements publics sur 170 sont concernés. Pour faciliter la reprise, les sapeurs-pompiers, les collectivités territoriales, les parents d’élèves et les communautés éducatives sont mobilisés. Toutefois, la remontée des nappes phréatiques complique parfois les opérations de pompage. Dans ces établissements, l’accueil des élèves pourrait être différé de 24 à 48 heures, selon l’évolution de la situation. Concernant le quantum horaire, le ministre se veut rassurant. Les 72 heures perdues devraient être récupérées grâce à des ajustements de l’organisation scolaire et à une mobilisation des acteurs de l’éducation. Moustapha Mamba Guirassy évoque notamment la possibilité de prolonger certaines activités pédagogiques afin de préserver le volume d’enseignement prévu pour l’année scolaire. Au-delà de cette rentrée, les perturbations climatiques relancent le débat sur l’adaptation du calendrier scolaire. Le ministre indique que plusieurs options ont été examinées, dont le maintien d’une date commune ou un démarrage différencié selon les académies. Pour l’année prochaine, une formule intermédiaire pourrait être envisagée, avec un décalage d’environ une semaine pour certaines académies, en fonction des contraintes locales. Cette éventuelle « semi-académisation » du calendrier reste à l’étude dans le cadre de la refondation du système éducatif. Elle devra notamment tenir compte des réalités climatiques, de l’organisation des examens et concours et du principe d’égalité des chances entre les élèves. Sur le plan matériel, le gouvernement annonce la mise à disposition d’un million de kits scolaires au profit des élèves et des établissements. Le ministre rappelle également la distribution de près de 60 000 tables-bancs l’année dernière et annonce un volume similaire pour cette année. Malgré les difficultés qui persistent dans certaines localités, les autorités maintiennent donc la rentrée du 12 octobre. L’enjeu reste désormais d’assurer une reprise dans des conditions satisfaisantes, tout en préservant la sécurité des élèves et la continuité des apprentissages.

items.title: When the Gospel Becomes a Weapon: The church, blackmail and the abuse of faith
items.description: Let me begin with a clear declaration. I am a Christian. I believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God and my Redeemer. I believe in the preaching of His gospel, and I support the mission of taking the Word of God to all nations. I believe the Church has a responsibility to spread the message of salvation, hope, love and repentance. I also believe that those entrusted with leading God’s people must be held to a higher standard of conduct, wisdom and integrity. My faith is not in conflict with my ability to question the conduct of religious leaders. In fact, I believe genuine faith should make us more willing to examine ourselves, confront wrongdoing and distinguish between the Word of God and the personal interests of those who claim to represent Him. It is against this background that I find some of the reactions by certain pastors to the new restriction on preaching and hawking in moving vehicles troubling. What should have been a reasonable public discussion about law, order, safety and the use of public spaces has, in some quarters, been presented as an attack on the Church and the gospel itself. But is every regulation that affects a religious activity an attack on Christianity? Must every government policy that inconveniences a pastor be read as persecution? And since when did the gospel become so fragile that a law regulating where and how people conduct their activities could threaten its very existence? The gospel is sacred, but not every activity conducted in its name is beyond question. What the regulation actually says Before anything else, the facts. Regulation 141 of the Road Traffic Regulations, 2026 (L.I. 2519) prohibits preaching and hawking inside public or commercial vehicles while they are in motion. The penalty is a fine of 10 to 50 penalty units, which the press has put at GH¢120 to GH¢600, imprisonment for up to eight months, or both. Three things are worth noticing. First, it applies to everyone. The same provision covers the trader selling goods on a moving bus and the preacher with a Bible in the aisle. Second, it does not touch preaching in churches, at crusade grounds, in markets or at lorry parks. It concerns the moving vehicle. Third, it is not new. The earlier Road Traffic Regulations, 2012 (L.I. 2180) carried a similar prohibition. What changed in recent weeks was enforcement. The reaction was swift. One prominent pastor told his congregation that the restriction was an attempt to gag the church. A pastor who is also a Member of Parliament appealed to the President to scrap what he called a bogus regulation that would jail innocent pastors and evangelists. On 9 October, the President responded that it is not true that the government has banned preaching in vehicles. No one, of any faith, may preach or sell in a moving vehicle, he said, but they may do so when it is stationary. The government has since reportedly suspended implementation, although the details of the suspension remain unclear. Suspension may calm the temperature. It does not settle the principle, and the principle is what I want to address. God is a God of order One of the things that makes some of these arguments difficult to understand is that the Bible itself places considerable emphasis on order. In 1 Corinthians 14:40, Paul instructs believers to let everything be done decently and in order. He was speaking about the gathered church, but the principle reaches beyond the four walls. It speaks to the broader Christian responsibility to conduct ourselves in ways that respect others and reflect the character of the God we serve. If God values order, why should Christians automatically resist reasonable attempts to regulate activities that affect public safety, traffic, noise, movement and the peaceful use of public spaces? We cannot insist that society must respect the Church while dismissing the legitimate interests of other members of that same society. Drivers, passengers, pedestrians, traders, workers and residents also have rights. A preacher’s desire to win souls does not erase the right of others to travel safely, conduct their business or enjoy a public space without undue interference. Indeed, if we believe that human life is sacred, then safety regulations should concern us. If we believe that God expects us to love our neighbours, then we must consider how our actions affect them. And if we believe in order, we should be prepared to demonstrate it in our public conduct. The question, therefore, should not be whether the government has the right to attack the gospel. It should be whether the particular law is reasonable, lawful, proportionate and necessary to address the problem it seeks to solve. That is where an intelligent discussion ought to begin. When regulation becomes persecution Some pastors have interpreted the restriction as an attempt to suppress Christianity. Others have extended the argument to include other religious groups, suggesting a wider attack on religious practice. I find this approach deeply problematic. A law regulating hawking or preaching in moving vehicles does not automatically amount to a prohibition on evangelism. A restriction on the place or manner in which a person conducts an activity is not necessarily a restriction on the belief that motivates it. There is a difference between preventing someone from preaching the gospel and regulating the circumstances under which that preaching takes place. Ghana’s Constitution draws the same line. Article 21(1)(c) guarantees the freedom to practise any religion and to manifest that practice. But Article 12(2) says that the fundamental rights and freedoms in the same chapter are enjoyed subject to respect for the rights and freedoms of others and for the public interest. Religious freedom is real, and it is not unlimited permission to do whatever one wishes in any public space. If a law genuinely discriminates against Christians, or prohibits them from practising their faith while allowing comparable activities by others, then the Church has every right to raise concerns. But such concerns must be established through evidence and careful reading of the law, not through emotional appeals designed to provoke fear among believers. We must be careful not to turn every disagreement with public policy into a spiritual battle between God and government. Such language can be particularly powerful in religious settings, because many believers trust their pastors and are reluctant to question their interpretations. When a pastor declares that a government action is an attack on God, some members may accept that conclusion without examining the facts. Others may feel guilty for supporting a law their religious leaders have condemned. Still others may become hostile towards public officials simply because they have been told that their actions threaten the Church. This is where the misuse of faith becomes dangerous. The pulpit should help people develop spiritual discernment, not discourage them from thinking critically. The gospel should enlighten the conscience, not frighten people into accepting every opinion expressed by a religious leader. Why drag other religions into the argument? I am equally concerned about attempts to turn this discussion into a debate about how other religious groups worship. Why should a conversation about the regulation of a particular activity become an opportunity to question the practices of people of different faiths? Ghana is a religiously diverse country. Christians, Muslims and people of other religious convictions live, work and conduct their affairs alongside one another. Our constitutional commitment to freedom of religion means we must respect the right of others to practise their faith, subject to the law. The danger of bringing other religions into this debate without a clear reason is that it shifts attention from the legal question to religious rivalry. It can encourage suspicion, deepen divisions and create the impression that public regulation is a contest over which religion has greater influence. That is a dangerous direction for a country such as Ghana. The proper question is whether the law is fair, whether it serves a legitimate public purpose and whether it respects the rights of everyone affected by it. If it is discriminatory, challenge the discrimination. If it is unreasonable, explain why. If it is poorly drafted, call for clarification or amendment. But do not turn a discussion about public order into an invitation to disparage the beliefs of others. Religious freedom cannot be meaningful if we defend it only when our own religious interests are involved. Why the law deserves serious consideration I believe the restriction deserves serious consideration because a moving vehicle is not a conventional place of worship. It is part of a transport system in which safety must take priority. Anything that distracts the driver, crowds the aisle, or exposes passengers to avoidable risk while the vehicle is moving deserves to be regulated, whether it is selling, preaching or anything else. The President’s clarification that preaching remains permitted when the vehicle is stationary shows that the target is the movement, not the message. There must also be room to distinguish between preaching that causes a public nuisance and preaching that is done peacefully without interfering with anyone’s rights. A reasonable law should be applied fairly and proportionately, and on that point, I think the critics have a fair question. The aim of the regulation is legitimate. Whether a prison term of up to eight months for a person who preaches on a bus is a proportionate way to achieve it is a different matter, and one on which reasonable people, including Christians who support the regulation’s purpose, can disagree. A fine, a warning, or simply a requirement to stop when the bus moves may protect road safety just as well. That is the kind of argument I would welcome from the pulpit: specific, evidence-based and respectful of the law’s purpose. It is a very different thing from claiming that the government is fighting God. My position is simple. The gospel must be preached, but the preaching of the gospel does not remove the need for public safety, lawful conduct and consideration for others. We cannot claim that our mission is to save lives while behaving carelessly towards the lives of those around us. Why don’t we preach in moving aeroplanes? I have a question for the pastors who have presented restrictions on preaching in moving vehicles as an attack on the gospel. When you travel on a commercial aeroplane, why don’t you stand up and preach to all the passengers? You may spend several hours on that flight. You may watch a film, listen to music, read a book or talk to the person beside you. Yet how often do you insist that the entire aircraft must become your congregation because you have a divine mandate to preach the Word? Why don’t you demand the right to take over the public address system and preach from take-off to landing? The answer should be obvious. An aeroplane operates under safety procedures and rules designed to protect everyone on board. The fact that a person is a pastor does not exempt him from the arrangements governing the flight. Watching a film does not mean that every other activity must be permitted, and permission to do one thing does not create an unrestricted right to do another. The point is not that a road vehicle and an aeroplane are identical. They are not. The point is that the setting in which an activity takes place matters. Safety, the rights of other passengers and the rules governing a particular environment cannot be dismissed because someone wishes to carry out a religious activity. If we understand that principle when we travel by air, why does it suddenly become hard to understand when public authorities regulate activities on our roads? Why don’t we preach in banking halls? Let me ask another question. Why don’t pastors walk into banking halls and begin preaching to customers waiting to transact business? After all, a bank is full of people. Some may be worried about their finances, some may be going through personal difficulties, and some may need hope and the message of salvation. If the presence of people who need the gospel were enough to justify preaching anywhere, why should a banking hall be excluded? Why don’t we insist that every bank allow pastors to preach to customers in the queue? The reason is that a banking hall has a specific purpose. People go there to conduct financial transactions, and the institution has responsibilities for security, privacy, orderly service and the protection of customers. A pastor’s good intentions do not automatically override those responsibilities. A person may have a genuine desire to share the gospel and still need to consider whether the place and manner are appropriate. The same reasoning applies to hospitals, courtrooms, classrooms and offices. Religious expression matters, but it must be weighed alongside the rights and legitimate interests of others. If we accept these boundaries in other settings, we should be able to discuss similar boundaries in public transport without immediately invoking persecution. The problem of religious blackmail What troubles me most is the tendency to use the gospel as a shield against reasonable questions and public accountability. I use the word blackmail deliberately, and I am describing a tactic, not condemning any individual. When a religious leader suggests that questioning his position amounts to fighting God, he is asking for an authority that no human being should possess. When disagreement with a pastor is presented as hostility towards Christianity, the discussion stops being about the merits of an argument. It becomes an attempt to silence criticism through fear. It places believers in a difficult position: agree with the pastor or risk being seen as an enemy of the gospel. It discourages honest discussion and allows personal opinions to take on the appearance of divine instruction. But a pastor is still a human being. Pastors can misunderstand laws, make poor arguments, pursue personal interests and respond emotionally to criticism. Their positions should be examined with the same care we apply to the claims of politicians, public officials and other leaders. The title of pastor does not make every opinion correct. A pulpit does not turn an interpretation into scripture. And the ability to quote the Bible does not mean that every argument made in its name is sound. The Church must be especially careful here, because religious leaders hold considerable influence over people who trust them. That influence must be exercised responsibly. We should be able to ask a pastor why he holds a particular position without being made to feel that we have offended God. We should be able to disagree with a religious leader without being threatened with spiritual consequences for questioning his legal or political opinions. Faith should produce discernment, humility and responsibility. It should not become a tool for protecting leaders from scrutiny. Let us practise what we preach I stand with the gospel any day. I support the preaching of Jesus Christ and the mission of taking His message to all nations. I believe the Church has a vital role in shaping moral values, offering hope and calling society to righteousness. But I also believe that those who preach the gospel must be willing to live by the principles they teach. If we preach humility, let us be humble enough to listen to arguments that challenge our views. If we preach truth, let us represent the law accurately. If we preach love, let us consider the rights and safety of people who do not share our faith. If we preach order, let us stop behaving as though rules should apply to everyone except religious leaders. And if we preach wisdom, let us reason before we react. The Church must not confuse its mission with the personal preferences of its leaders. A regulation affecting a particular activity does not automatically threaten Christianity. If a law is unjust, let us demonstrate its injustice. If it infringes on religious freedom, let us make that case with facts, sound legal reasoning and constitutional principles. If it is reasonable, let us have the courage to acknowledge that, even when it places limits on activities some of us would prefer to conduct without restriction. There is no shame in a pastor admitting that a law serves a legitimate public purpose. There is no loss of faith in acknowledging that the rights of others matter. And there is no betrayal of the gospel in insisting that religious leaders should act responsibly. What we must stop doing is using the name of God to frighten people into agreement, presenting every disagreement as persecution, and dragging the gospel into controversies that can be settled by reasoned discussion. Christianity does not need manipulation to survive. The truth does not need intimidation to defend itself. I will continue to stand for Jesus Christ, for the preaching of His gospel and for the freedom to practise my faith. But I will also stand for reason, public order, fairness and accountability. I will question religious leaders when I believe they are wrong, just as I will question political leaders and public officials when they abuse their positions. My Christianity does not require me to surrender my judgement to another human being. Let us preach the gospel. Let us win souls. Let us defend religious freedom. But let us also respect the law, consider the rights of others and be honest about our motives. And above all, let us stop pretending that every criticism of a pastor is an attack on God, stop using the gospel to blackmail believers into silence, and start practising what the Bible teaches. The gospel deserves to be preached with conviction, defended with wisdom and lived with integrity. Dr Michael Kubi is a lecturer at the University of Professional Studies, Accra, a governance consultant and an author.

items.title: Indian court releases 'cockroach' movement leaders from detention
items.description: Leaders of India’s youth-led “cockroach” movement on Sunday pledged to press on with protests against the country’s election commissioner, hours after they were released from detention, as authorities sought to thwart major demonstrations in New Delhi. The rallies in the capital come after weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision that critics say could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party. The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing. Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and two other leaders were released Sunday, one day after they were detained when they landed in New Delhi to take part in a protest at the Jantar Mantar site in the heart of the city. Thousands of protesters have been detained since Saturday, according to the group and media reports. “We will not back down,” Saurav Das, another top CJP leader, told reporters after his release. “We urge people to come out and carry out peaceful protests,” he added, vowing to continue until Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns. Smaller rallies took place in Delhi on Sunday. Dozens of protesters were detained near Jantar Mantar, which remained blocked off, AFP journalists witnessed. Police have not commented on the detentions. Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said at least 16 journalists had also been detained, calling the police actions “unacceptable”. “Covering events of public interest is not a crime,” RSF said in a statement. “It is their job.” In July, protests organised by the CJP over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi’s administration. ‘Important show up’ Ahead of Saturday’s rally, authorities mounted a sweeping security operation across the capital, shutting down metro stations and more than 200 trains while imposing a ban on public gatherings in several areas. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel remained deployed on Sunday, but metro stations reopened and previously restricted mobile services were restored. “I was detained for 10 hours yesterday,” said Aarti, 37, who gave only one name. “I have come again today because it is important to show up.” The protest leaders were released on the condition that they would maintain “peace for one year”, Ratna Singh, the CJP’s head lawyer, said in a social media post. The Supreme Court, hearing petitions challenging Saturday’s detentions and other security measures, directed the authorities to ensure protesters gathering peacefully were not detained illegally. “Detention shall only be after following a legal procedure,” Justice Joymalya Bagchi said in oral remarks. The court also ordered authorities to ensure there was no disruption to internet connectivity as seen on Saturday. ‘An embarrassment to India’ The CJP has emerged as one of the most significant political challenges to Modi during his third term in power, winning millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May as a satirical party. Soon after his release, the CJP’s Dipke took aim at Modi, calling him “an embarrassment to India”. “Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” he said in a social media post. The revision of voter rolls resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports. Critics say the measure has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, potentially benefiting Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. Election authorities say the move was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries. The detention of protesters on Saturday triggered sharp criticism and accusations that Modi’s government was stifling dissent. The UN human rights office called for the immediate and unconditional release of all those “arbitrarily detained” in Delhi — a comment the Indian government called “misplaced”. Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition Congress party, said he was planning to march to the Supreme Court on Monday with “every single person who believes in democracy”. “There is nothing to fear,” he said on social media. “These cowards can do absolutely nothing to us. “

items.title: Petrol: Marketers hike pump price in Abuja, Lagos by N29/litre
items.description: By Udeme Akpan & Obas Esiedesa, Abuja Days after the Federal Government announced measures to cushion the impact of rising fuel prices on consumers, petroleum marketers have increased petrol pump prices by up to N29 per litre in Abuja. Checks across the nation’s capital on Sunday showed that AA Rano and AYM Shafa increased their pump prices to N1,409 per litre from N1,380 per litre last week. Similarly, an NNPC Retail outlet in Azhata, Jikwoyi District, increased its pump price to N1,405 per litre from N1,380, while MRS, a partner retail outlet of Dangote Refinery, raised its price to N1,405 per litre from N1,370. The increases came despite the Federal Government’s petrol discount initiative, under which the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) extended its N66-per-litre discount until October 31, 2026. The discount, introduced on October 1 to mark Nigeria’s 66th Independence Anniversary, reduced NNPC Retail’s N1,405 pump price to N1,339 per litre for customers who pay digitally through its mobile application. The Federal Government said the initiative was being funded through NNPC Retail’s decision to forgo its profit margin rather than through public funds, stressing that it did not amount to a return to petrol subsidy. In Lagos, some stations in Ikorodu and other locations sold petrol at N1,360 per litre, while outlets in Coker, Orile and Second Rainbow retailed the product at N1,350 per litre. However, some independent oil marketers sold petrol at between N1,360 and N1,400 per litre, depending on location. The latest increases reflect continuing pressure on domestic petrol prices following the rise in global crude oil prices amid the Middle East conflict. In a statement, NNPC Limited said its discount was intended to provide relief to consumers during the period of elevated global market uncertainty. It stated: “We recognise that higher petrol prices affect everyday life, from the cost of commuting to the expenses of running a business. We understand the strain on families and livelihoods, and this discount is intended to provide direct relief to customers during this difficult period. “Following the statement by the Honourable Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, on 8 October 2026, NNPC Limited reiterates its commitment to working with the government and stakeholders to cushion the impact of rising fuel prices on households, businesses and the wider economy. “Before the announcement, NNPC Limited had introduced a sales discount on 1 October 2026 to commemorate Nigeria’s 66th Independence Anniversary. This will now continue until 31 October 2026 across NNPC Retail stations nationwide. This discount is a customer relief initiative and does not represent the reintroduction of petroleum subsidy. “This initiative supports the government’s responsible and proactive approach to providing practical relief to Nigerians during a period of heightened global market uncertainty. The initiative applies to NNPC Retail outlets and does not establish a uniform national pump price or alter the market-based pricing framework applicable to petroleum products. “NNPC Limited remains committed to reliable product supply and collaboration with the government and stakeholders to help ease the burden on Nigerians. We therefore urge the public to disregard any interpretation of this discount as a subsidy restoration.” It added: “We appreciate Nigerians’ continued patronage and support, and remain committed to clear communication about our products, prices and customer initiatives.” The post Petrol: Marketers hike pump price in Abuja, Lagos by N29/litre appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ADC campaign to police: You can’t arrest hunger by stopping rally
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has accused the Kano State Police Command of suppressing dissent after operatives allegedly disrupted a ‘Tinubu Must Go’ rally and arrested the owner of the venue where it was held. The council said the incident at The Avenue Event Center, Kano, exposed the tension between the government’s democratic claims and citizens’ right to protest, warning that police action could neither silence public frustration nor erase anger over hunger, insecurity and the rising cost of living. In a statement on Sunday by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, the council said the rally, led by Barrister Abba Hikima and organised by concerned youths, was disrupted when police operatives barricaded the venue and allegedly intimidated participants. “This is not democracy. This is tyranny. For how long will the APC continue to use the police to suppress dissenting voices?” Ologbondiyan queried. The ADC-PCC expressed particular outrage over the reported arrest of the event centre owner for allegedly allowing the gathering, questioning why a business owner should face arrest for providing a venue for a peaceful assembly. “The message from Kano is loud and clear: Nigerians are tired, hungry and angry. You can stop a rally and arrest a venue owner, but you cannot arrest hunger in the land. You cannot barricade the anger and frustration of over 200 million people,” Ologbondiyan said. The council accused the APC-led government of misdirecting its priorities, arguing that the effort deployed to stop the rally should instead be channelled into tackling insecurity, banditry and the cost-of-living crisis. “If the APC government had deployed the same energy it used to stop a peaceful rally at The Avenue Event Center to tackle insecurity, banditry and the excruciating cost of living, Nigeria would be a safer and more prosperous nation,” he added. The ADC-PCC commended Hikima and the participating youths for standing their ground despite the reported police intimidation. It also urged the Inspector-General of Police and the Kano State Police Command to ensure the immediate and unconditional release of the venue owner, if still in custody, and refrain from actions that could turn the police into an instrument of political oppression. The council further called on civil society organisations, human rights groups and the international community to monitor what it described as an erosion of democratic freedoms. “The right to protest is not a privilege granted by the police or the APC; it is a right guaranteed by the Constitution. No amount of intimidation will stop Nigerians from demanding change,” the statement said. The post ADC campaign to police: You can’t arrest hunger by stopping rally appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027: Enugu Govt alleges opposition plot to import armed thugs, bandits
items.description: …Denies government involvement in NDC airport, secretariat incidents S ays Mbah’s performance more than enough to win free, fair election The Enugu State Government said it has uncovered alleged plans by some opposition elements to import armed thugs and bandits into the state to create panic and a false sense of insecurity ahead of the 2027 general elections. The Secretary to the State Government (SSG), Prof. Chidiebere Onyia, made these known on Sunday while addressing a press conference at the Government House, Enugu, on the incidents involving the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport and the party’s state secretariat in Enugu on Saturday. Onyia denied any involvement of the government or the Governor’s Chief Security Officer, Ifeanyi Osondu, in both incidents, describing the airport confrontation as a matter between the NDC and federal authorities, while noting that the shooting incident at the party’s secretariat was under police investigation. According to the SSG, the government’s preliminary findings indicated that the airport incident followed the NDC’s attempt to hold what it described as a “Grand Statewide Campaign Flag-off 2026” at the facility without securing the necessary approval from the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN). He said the party had published notices inviting its members and supporters to the event, including on the Facebook page of its governorship candidate in the state. Onyia explained that the police had advised the party to obtain FAAN’s approval before security personnel could be deployed to the airport for the event. “Further findings, however, revealed that the NDC did not secure the approval of FAAN to host a grand statewide rally at its facility. Security agencies, therefore, advised the organisers of the rally to rethink it,” he said. The SSG alleged that the party proceeded to mobilise its members to the airport and attempted to gain entry into the facility, resulting in a confrontation with airport authorities. He said security agencies intervened to disperse the “riotous” party members and restore order around the airport, which he described as a strategic national asset. Onyia added that the state government’s account was consistent with the statement issued by the Enugu State Police Command on Sunday. NDC Secretariat Shooting On the shooting incident at the NDC state secretariat in the GRA area of Enugu, the SSG said security reports had established that a violent clash occurred at the party’s office and that the police were investigating the matter. The SSG disputed reports alleging fatalities, stating that the government’s findings indicated that no death had occurred in the incident. He disclosed that a 43-year-old man, identified as Ifeanyi Nworie, sustained a gunshot wound and was taken to the Enugu State University Teaching Hospital, Park Lane, where he was stabilised before being transferred to the National Orthopaedic Hospital, Enugu, for further examination. “We can, therefore, authoritatively report that there were no deaths as falsely claimed by some reports and NDC leaders,” he said. Onyia also faulted allegations that the Governor’s Chief Security Officer was present at the party secretariat and supervised the shooting, maintaining that the official was with Governor Peter Mbah at the Teachers Grassroots Movement mega rally at Okpara Square, Enugu, at the time of the incident. The SSG further criticised the reported holding of a minute’s silence for an individual he said was still alive, describing it as an attempt to mislead the public for political advantage. Reaffirming the state government’s position, Onyia said Governor Mbah had sworn to protect the lives and property of all residents, irrespective of their religious beliefs or political affiliations, and condemned. He said the administration’s ambition to grow Enugu into a $30 billion economy and make it a preferred destination for investment, business, tourism and living depended significantly on sustained peace and security. According to him, this informed the government’s substantial investments in security infrastructure and operations over the past three years. “Consequently, the Enugu State Government strongly condemns in its entirety any form of violence, including politically induced violence in the state. We welcome healthy debate and freedom of association and peaceful assembly,” he said. He, however, urged political parties and their candidates to exercise restraint and embrace issue-based campaigns ahead of the 2027 elections. The SSG said democratic rights should be exercised responsibly, arguing that political parties ought to serve as models of decorum and integrity. He questioned the decision to announce a statewide campaign flag-off at the airport and without the approval of the relevant authorities. “Without holding brief for FAAN, is it not sheer rascality to attempt to hold a “Grand Statewide Campaign Flag-off 2026” of the NDC at the airport as publicised by the party and its gubernatorial candidate, especially without the approval by the appropriate authorities? “Is it not equally gross mischief and a sign of political desperation to hold a minute silence for a living person, just to mislead the public for political traction?” he queried. Onyia accused opposition elements in the state of attempting to create the impression that Enugu was unsafe and that the government was intolerant of opposing political parties. He alleged that some opposition groups had been attributing internal disagreements and violent clashes to the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the state. As an example, he cited the September 12, 2026 incident at Obuofia in Nkanu West Local Government Area, claiming that investigations had identified the alleged perpetrators, who were being prosecuted by the police. The SSG described the opposition as factionalised and alleged that some of its members were seeking to draw the state government into controversies for political relevance. Onyia also reiterated the government’s allegation that some opposition elements were plotting to bring armed thugs and bandits into Enugu to create panic and undermine public confidence in the state’s security ahead of the 2027 general elections. “We, however, make bold to say that the peace and security we have achieved in Enugu State in the last three years, and at huge material costs and sacrifices by our security agents, are non-negotiable and irreversible,” he said. The SSG said the Mbah administration remained committed to protecting citizens’ democratic rights, including the freedom to campaign for and vote for candidates of their choice in the forthcoming elections. He described the right of residents to elect their leaders through free, fair and credible polls as fundamental to the state’s democratic development. Onyia added that the government was confident of securing a second term for Mbah based on what it described as the governor’s performance and delivery on campaign promises. “Indeed, these inalienable rights of Ndi Enugu to elect their leaders in free, fair and credible polls are our surest hope for re-election come 2027,” he said. He added that the administration had no reason to resort to desperate measures, maintaining that its record in office would be the basis for seeking a renewed mandate from the electorate. The post 2027: Enugu Govt alleges opposition plot to import armed thugs, bandits appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Air France dans l'embarras face à la demande d'Israël de filtrer les nationalités du personnel navigant
items.description: La compagnie aérienne Air France demande à son personnel navigant de 31 nationalités de se retirer de lui-même des vols à destination d'Israël. La société se plie ainsi, à sa manière, à une directive des autorités israéliennes, après la tentative d'attentat du co-pilote d'un vol Flydubai, le 30 septembre. Dans cette directive, sont pointés du doigt les nationalités de 31 pays n'ayant pas de relations diplomatiques avec l'État hébreu. Les doubles nationalités sont aussi concernées.

items.title: Tivaouane : deux jeunes tués dans une collision entre une moto et un camion
items.description: Un grave accident de la circulation s'est produit dans la nuit du 11 au 12 octobre 2026, aux environs de 22h30, à hauteur du Centre hospitalier Seydi El Hadj Malick Sy de Tivaouane. L'accident a impliqué une moto de type Jakarta et un camion plateau de marque Renault. Selon les premiers renseignements recueillis, la moto était conduite par Cheikh Yaba Diouf, né le 8 mars 2005 à Tivaouane, conducteur de moto Jakarta, qui avait à son bord un passager, Babacar Niang, né le 20 janvier 2007 à Tivaouane. La moto est entrée en collision avec le camion qui roulait en sens inverse. Le camion était conduit par El Hadj Fallou Seck, âgé de 50 ans, domicilié à Touba. Suite à l'accident, il a été placé en garde à vue au commissariat urbain de Tivaouane pour les besoins de l'enquête. Le bilan est lourd. Les deux occupants de la moto ont succombé à leurs blessures après leur évacuation par les sapeurs-pompiers de Tivaouane vers l'hôpital Mame Abdou Aziz Sy Dabakh. Une enquête a été ouverte par le commissariat urbain de Tivaouane pour déterminer les circonstances exactes de l'accident. Ibrahima NDIAYE (Correspondant)

items.title: Amnesty condemns police blockade of ‘Tinubu-Must-Go’ event in Kano
items.description: Amnesty International Nigeria has condemned the alleged blocking of a “Tinubu-Must-Go” event in Kano State, accusing the police of violating the rights to freedom of association and peaceful assembly. The human rights organisation disclosed this in a post on its X platform on Sunday, saying heavily armed police officers blocked both ends of the road leading to the venue of the event. Amnesty described the action as an unlawful restriction on peaceful political activities and called on the Nigeria Police Force to desist from what it termed a reckless violation of human rights. “The Nigeria Police must desist from such reckless violation of human rights. It is perfectly within the rights of supporters of all candidates and all political parties to carry out peaceful political activities,” the organisation said. It maintained that the police had a responsibility to facilitate peaceful political gatherings, regardless of the political party or candidate being supported or opposed. “The duty of the police is to facilitate peaceful conduct of such political gatherings — no matter the political party or candidate being supported or opposed,” Amnesty said. The organisation stressed that freedom of association and peaceful assembly was not exclusive to any political party or its supporters. It further described the Kano incident as part of what it called a troubling pattern of police repression targeting opposition members in different parts of the country. According to Amnesty, repeated attacks and intimidation against opposition supporters could undermine their ability to associate freely and organise peaceful public gatherings. The organisation did not provide further details about the event or the police operation in its post. The post Amnesty condemns police blockade of ‘Tinubu-Must-Go’ event in Kano appeared first on Vanguard News .
