items.title: Trente jeunes formés pour mieux valoriser les productions
items.description: Avec la formation d’une cohorte de 30 jeunes (80% de femmes) ayant reçu leurs attestations ce samedi 10 octobre, Ziguinchor prépare ainsi une riposte durable contre le gaspillage alimentaire. Portée par le Programme alimentaire mondial (Pam) et ses partenaires, cette initiative inclusive entend transformer les pertes post-récoltes en opportunités d’emploi et renforcer la souveraineté alimentaire en Casamance. ZIGUINCHOR- Dans le sud du pays, l’abondance des récoltes ne garantit pas toujours la disponibilité des produits agricoles tout au long de l’année. Faute d’infrastructures adaptées pour leur conservation et leur transformation, une partie de la production disparaît avant d’atteindre les consommateurs, tandis que certains produits deviennent rares pendant la période de soudure. Pour inverser cette tendance, 30 bénéficiaires viennent d’achever une formation destinée à préparer la mise en place d’une unité spécialisée dans la gestion et la valorisation des productions locales. Sélectionnés parmi plus de 400 candidats, ils ont suivi un programme intensif de 30 jours, du 9 septembre au 10 octobre, dans le cadre du projet « Salouma ». Cette initiative vise à préparer la future Unité de gestion des pertes post-récoltes (Ugpp), appelée à soutenir les acteurs agricoles tout en favorisant la création d’emplois. Pour William Diatta, chef du bureau du PAM pour la zone sud, cette démarche marque une évolution dans l’accompagnement des communautés. « Au-delà de l’assistance alimentaire, nous voulons renforcer les capacités des populations afin qu’elles gagnent en autonomie et participent activement au développement de leurs localités », explique-t-il. Pour préparer cette nouvelle étape, l’ITD a privilégié une approche associant développement personnel et apprentissage professionnel. Son directeur, Mbagnick Faye, estime que la confiance en soi, le leadership et le sens des responsabilités sont indispensables à la réussite du projet. « Avant de transmettre les compétences techniques, nous avons travaillé sur le développement personnel, la confiance en soi et l’engagement, car il faut croire en ses capacités pour exploiter efficacement les outils disponibles », indique-t-il. Une initiative placée sous le signe de l’inclusion Entrepreneuriat, gestion financière et exercices pratiques etc., font partie des formations dispensées. Ce programme se distingue par sa dimension sociale : 80 % des participants sont des femmes et des personnes en situation de handicap figurent également parmi les bénéficiaires. Pour Claudine Géma Gomis, cette ouverture renforce la portée de l’initiative, dont les retombées pourront profiter à l’ensemble de la chaîne agricole. « Cette initiative ne concerne pas uniquement les personnes formées. Les producteurs, les commerçants, les transformateurs et les détaillants pourront également bénéficier des services proposés pour mieux conserver et valoriser leurs produits », explique-t-elle. Responsable de la cohorte, Ibrahima Sorry Diallo souligne l’importance de cette démarche face aux pénuries saisonnières. « Après les périodes d’abondance, certains produits deviennent difficiles à trouver. La conservation et la transformation permettront de prolonger leur disponibilité et de réduire ces pénuries », affirme-t-il. La diversité des profils, notamment en comptabilité, commerce, transformation et gestion, devrait contribuer à la bonne marche des activités. Avec le soutien du PAM, de la Fondation Mastercard et de l’ITD, ce projet entend ainsi de la lutte contre les pertes post-récoltes un levier de développement économique. Gaustin DIATTA (Correspondant)

items.title: Kaolack: La Flamme olympique illumine le Cœur de Ville
items.description: Après Fatick, la caravane de la Flamme olympique a fait escale ce samedi 10 octobre 2026 à Kaolack où les populations ont communié autour des valeurs de paix et d’unité. Une cérémonie haute en couleur, marquée par la mobilisation des acteurs sportifs, culturels et des autorités territoriales. Le Cœur de Ville de Kaolack a servi de cadre à une cérémonie riche en couleurs, à l’occasion du passage de la caravane de la Flamme olympique dans la capitale du Saloum. Athlètes, autorités locales, acteurs culturels et sportifs se sont réunis pour célébrer les valeurs d’unité, de paix et de dépassement de soi portées par le mouvement olympique. Dans une ambiance festive, rythmée par les chants traditionnels et les acclamations du public, le maire de Kaolack, Serigne Mboup, a exprimé sa fierté d’accueillir la Flamme olympique dans cette partie du Saloum. « L’arrivée de la Flamme olympique au cœur de notre ville est bien plus qu’un symbole sportif. C’est la reconnaissance de la vitalité, de l’hospitalité et du potentiel de la jeunesse de Kaolack. En accueillant cette flamme, nous faisons briller la culture du Saloum aux yeux du monde entier », a déclaré l’édile. La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence de l’adjoint au gouverneur chargé du développement, Mouhamadou Habib Kamara et du président du Conseil départemental, Ahmed Youssouf Benjelloune. À cette occasion, Serigne Mboup a réaffirmé l’engagement de la municipalité à promouvoir la pratique sportive chez les jeunes et à moderniser les infrastructures de la ville. Un engagement qui, selon lui, participe à la valorisation du potentiel de la jeunesse et au rayonnement de Kaolack. Parmi les temps forts de la cérémonie, la réception de la Flamme par Me Guedel Ndiaye, pour lancer les festivités. Suivra ensuite une petite tournée à travers quelques artères de la ville. De retour au Cœur de Ville, l’honneur est revenu à Amadou Gallo Fall pour allumer le chaudron, sous les applaudissements nourris du public. Après cette étape kaolackoise, la caravane de la Flamme olympique poursuit son périple dans la zone centre, avec une prochaine escale annoncée à Kaffrine. Mamadou THIAM ( Correspondant)

items.title: Do Human Beings Have Souls?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube The majority of Americans believe that every human being has an immaterial soul, and they tend to base their sense of human dignity and equality on this belief. Yet the culture at large often operates under the assumption that physical reality is all there is. Which view is correct? In this episode of The Permanent Questions , self-described “spookiest” David Brooks talks with Shelly Kagan, a best-selling philosopher who insists souls do not exist—and that we don’t need them in order to embrace the wonder and mystery of human experience. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: I think the essayist Meghan O’Gieblyn was accurately capturing parts of America when, in her book God, Human, Animal, Machine , she wrote, “It is meaningless to speak of the soul in the 21st century. It has become a dead metaphor, one of those words that survive in language long after a culture has lost faith in the concept." Yet here’s the funny thing: According to the Pew Research Center, 85 percent of Americans say that they have a soul. They really do believe they have a mystical, immaterial, spooky, ghostlike thing at the center of who they are. And I have a confession to make: I’m one of those people. Furthermore, this metaphorical and spiritual meaning of the word soul is pretty central to the way I see the world. Long before I ever believed in God, I was firmly convinced that each person you meet has some piece of themselves that has no size, weight, color, or shape, but gives them infinite value and dignity. In today’s conversation, we’re gonna address the question: Do humans have souls? I’ve laid my cards on the table. I think they do. We’re gonna be joined by Shelly Kagan, and he does not think we do. Kagan is the Clark Professor of Philosophy at Yale University. For over 40 years, stretching back to his days at the University of Illinois, Chicago, he has taught a course on death to undergrads, which, naturally enough, takes up the subject of the soul. Shelly Kagan (from lecture): Last time, I distinguished between two ways in which thinking about the facts about the nature of death could influence our behavior. On the one hand, it could give us reasons to behave or respond differently, and on the other hand, it could merely cause us to behave differently. The course has become globally famous because it’s on YouTube. Those lectures have been seen 33 million times in China alone. Part of his success is his intellect, but part derives from the fact that for a guy who doesn’t believe in enchantment, he’s a completely enchanting guy. I’m pleased to welcome Shelly Kagan to this table. Shelly Kagan, welcome to The Permanent Questions . We are honored to have you here. Now, there’s a chapter in your life I’m confused about. It concerns the time you go to Wesleyan in 1972. You grew up in Skokie, Illinois, right? Shelly Kagan: That’s correct. Brooks: And you go to Wesleyan, and you’re a religion major for some period of that time. But you also read John Stuart Mill’s Utilitarianism , which suggests to me that you’re trending in the direction you’re trending, which we’ll talk about. But then in your senior year, you apply to rabbinic school. So in my mind, you’re trending toward a utilitarian, maybe non-believing form of life, and then you apply to become a rabbi. What’s up with that? Kagan: I had planned to be a rabbi starting at some point in high school, and that was what I anticipated all through college. As you say, I applied to rabbinical school, a particular rabbinical school, in fall of my senior year. I got the rejection letter, spring of my senior year. So I graduated from college and was suddenly in the situation that most of my friends had been in for four years, asking myself, So what do I want to do with my life? I thought I had known what I wanted to do with my life. But I had already come into college knowing I was also interested in philosophy, which, as it happens, I’d gotten into through Judaica. Brooks: I guess my question is: Did you believe in God, and you thought, Well, I’d like to serve God by being a rabbi ? Kagan: Well, I believed in the importance of Judaism, and I suppose any traditional Jew will say something like, “I believe in God.” But what it is to believe in God—as I imagine you know—from the Jewish point of view, that’s left much more up to you. Judaism doesn’t have a central set of religious dogmas. How you interpret this, as well as other central Jewish thoughts, like revelation—there are rival thinkers. Judaism was important to me through college. Judaism stayed important to me after I got rejected from rabbinical school. After college, I asked myself, Should I reapply to rabbinical school? Should I get a secular Judaic degree? Or—and this was literally the very first time the question ever crossed my mind— Maybe I should become a philosopher. Since I thought I had known what I was going to do, the question had literally never occurred to me. Brooks: When you thought about philosophy, did you think, I just wanna talk about big ideas , or is it, Like being a rabbi, I’m sort of ministering to people’s minds ? Kagan: I think it’s not a coincidence that of all the different topics in philosophy, the area I ended up specializing in is ethics and moral philosophy. I continue to think about questions about value, which were certainly the things that most drove me to wanting to be a rabbi as well. Brooks: Now you teach this famous course on death, which has become internationally known. It’s unlike a lot of courses, where the professor offers: “Here’s this person’s view, here’s that person’s view, here’s this person’s view.” As I understand the course on death, and I’ve seen it on YouTube, you say, “Here’s my point of view. What do you think?” Could you summarize the argument of that course? Kagan: As you say, in a number of classes, including several of my own classes, when I teach introductory ethics, I say, “Here’s four or five prominent views. Here are the arguments for; here’s the arguments against." I try to keep my cards pretty close to my chest. In the death class, as I began to put it together, I decided that wasn’t the way to go. I wasn’t going to pretend. I say on the very first day, “Here’s a bunch of things that lots of people believe about death, and I’m going to spend the semester arguing, trying to convince you that they’re not so.” I try to be fair—I hope I’m fair—to the views that I’m rejecting, but I don’t hide what my considered conclusions are. So as I say, most people, at least lots of people, believe in a soul. By that term, using it as a piece of jargon, I mean that we have some immaterial, nonphysical part of us, maybe the essence of what we really are, and that thing can survive the death of our body. It’s good to believe in such a thing because mortality is bad. It would be good to live forever. If it’s not true, then death is something terrifying. Suicide never makes sense. There’s a variety of views like this. Death is very mysterious. What exactly is it? Something we can’t know, can’t really get our head around. Over the course of the semester, I try to argue that there is no soul, that there’s nothing especially mysterious about death or dying, that immortality would not be desirable, that fear of death does not make sense, that there are circumstances in which suicide can be rational. I work through the various positions and try to lay out what strike me as the most promising arguments for the views before turning around and explaining why I think those arguments aren’t compelling. Brooks: I want to get into the substance of this, but I’m just curious: These are undergrads; they’re 20 years old, 21, 19. Why are they interested in death? It’s so far away. Kagan: When I first started teaching the class—that was before I came to Yale. I was at the University of Illinois Chicago. I taught the class a handful of times there, maybe four times in the nine years I was there, and almost nobody took it. But when I came to Yale, I thought, Well, it’s worth trying it again . Now, at the time, this is more than 30 years ago, because there was no preregistration, I had no idea how many people would show up. I thought, Maybe 50 people will show up. To be safe, I’ll run off 75 copies of the syllabus . Three hundred and twenty odd people showed up, and I realized I’ve hit a nerve here in ways that I really hadn’t anticipated. Of course, it’s a subject that everybody cares about. It’s a subject that everybody thinks about. Interestingly enough, from the pedagogical perspective, as a philosophy professor, it’s a wonderful subject for an introductory class because it allows you to move from questions in metaphysics and epistemology and value theory and ethics and philosophy of mind and the like. Brooks: Do they push back? Are they offended by what you’re saying? Do they embrace what you’re saying? Kagan: I tell them that my goal in the class—although in some sense is to persuade them of a variety of claims, what’s most important to me is that they end up thinking through these issues. If they’ve genuinely given the matter thought and have come away disagreeing with me, that’s great. Philosophical questions are ones in which—this is a theme throughout all of my classes—reasonable people can disagree. So the class is really an invitation to think about some really important questions. Brooks: We reasonably disagree whether people have souls. Even when I didn’t believe in God, which was most of my adult life, the way I would put it is that each of us has a piece of us that has no size, weight, color, or shape, but gives us infinite value and dignity. That accords with my sense of just looking around the world—that everybody I meet seems to have some sacred dignity. So if that’s my sense of where human dignity comes from … Kagan: Let’s start with no size. What was it? No size, no shape? Brooks: Color or shape. Kagan: So let’s start with something totally trivial. You believe that seven times eight equals 56. Does that thought have color? Does it have weight? Does it have shape? Well, presumably not. In philosopher jargon, that’s some sort of category mistake to think that things like that have to have color and shape, like this glass of water. The very first thing we have to understand is that you can believe, as I do believe, that I’m just a material object and that you’re just a material object—the people watching this show are just material objects—and so we have size, color, shape. Not everything that’s true of us is helpfully described in those terms. What I think is that you’re a material object that is able to think. You’re able to think about simple mathematical facts, and depending on how far you got in your math education— Brooks: You hit the limit of it right there. Kagan: You’re able to think about more complicated facts. You’re able to make plans. You’re able to communicate with me. And the question is: Can we point to various properties like that and explain how a material object can have the ability to think, to be creative, to fall in love, and so forth? There are aspects about us which give us a special kind of—you used the Kantian phrase— dignity. I’m happy to talk that way. I don’t think that’s a mistake. I don’t think that gives us reason to think that there’s something nonphysical about us. You would then have to ask the question: By virtue of what is it true that we count morally? And this is a contested philosophical question. If you want, I can rattle off three theories, but I’m not sure how much in the weeds you wanna get. Brooks: Yeah, let’s go there. Kagan: Let me start with one that I think is probably part of the story but won’t get you all the way to dignity—at least all the way to dignity in the sense I think you mean it. As I say to my intro ethics students, if I were to bring in a cat, douse it with gasoline, and then set it on fire, and then it shrieks in agony, most of us would agree—maybe not everybody, but most of us would agree—that that would be wrong. It counts morally. It’s a stray cat, let’s pretend, so I’m not hurting its owner, right? I’m doing something wrong to the cat. The cat counts in its own right. By virtue of what? A natural plausible thought is that it counts by virtue of the fact that it can feel pleasure and pain. I think that’s true about cats. One might think it isn’t true about animals. That’s up to you. But suppose it’s what most of us do think, that cats feel pleasure and pain. That makes them count in a certain way, and it would explain why it would be wrong for me to douse one in gasoline and set it on fire. In part, it would also explain why it would be wrong for me to douse you with gasoline and set you on fire. So that’s one story. I don’t think that’s probably the whole story and maybe not the most important part of the story. You used the Kantian word dignity . Immanuel Kant, a great German philosopher, thought that our moral standing, which differentiates us from animals—Kantians have a hard time explaining why animals should count, too—but Kantians basically think it has something to do with our freedom, with our rationality, with our autonomy, with the ability to set ends for ourselves, to decide how we wanna act, and to reason about what goals and actions make sense. I find that a very plausible and attractive idea. You’re an autonomous being. The etymology here is “auto,” self , “nomos,” law . You’re the kind of being that can give laws to yourself, decide for yourself how you wanna live. By virtue of your being an autonomous being, you count in a special way. Animals that merely feel pleasure and pain but don’t have that kind of freedom; they count, I think, in a lesser way. So I think that you have that special moral status. We can use the word dignity to try to mark it. There’d be more wrong about setting you on fire than merely the fact that it would hurt. If I killed you painlessly, it would still be wrong, because as an autonomous being, you’ve set various goals for yourself. There are things you want to accomplish with your life. It’s a controversial philosophical question, but I don’t see why bringing that in necessarily means you have to bring in a soul, if by a soul we mean something nonphysical, immaterial, distinct from our body. Just like we need to be able to tell a story about how a material object can believe seven times eight equals 56, we’ll need a story—it’ll be more complicated—about how a material being can come to set goals and reconsider them and reevaluate them and so forth. Brooks: You said Kant believes humans have dignity. Do you? Would you say that humans have—I used the term “infinite dignity,” which is going up to 11? Kagan: I will confess, dignity is not one of the words that typically I’ll find myself using. But I’m not troubled by using it. What is it that one means when one talks about a person having dignity? I’m perfectly comfortable talking that way, but it’s just a placeholder. Then we have to start talking about what are the sorts of things that come with being a creature with dignity. How it can be treated, how it should not be treated, what things it’s permissible to do to it, what things you have to do for it, what things you may not do to it. To throw out more jargon, Kant was a deontologist. He thought that if you took these notions of morality being grounded in autonomy, generating a certain kind of dignity that demands respect, that this leads to a family of theories within moral philosophy called deontological views. According to deontologists, there are certain actions that it would be wrong to do to somebody even if the results would be better if you were to do them. Against that, there are rival schools of thought that say, “No, if results really would be better, it becomes permissible." My own view is that Kant was right about morality being grounded in autonomy, freedom, rationality. He was wrong in believing that this leads to deontology as opposed to—to introduce another piece of jargon—a more consequence-oriented approach. But I’m happy to go with Kant about the foundations of ethics, because not everybody thinks autonomy is the core of ethics. Brooks: I was gonna go there. Kagan: Thomas Hobbes, another great philosopher. He’s British—1650, I think that’s when Leviathan gets published, something like that. Hobbes thought the ultimate basis of morality has to do with the fact that, roughly speaking, we can hurt each other, and we need help from one another. If we try to imagine a world with no moral requirements, we’ll all be at each other’s throats. You have some food, I’ll cut your throat, if I can. When you’re looking the other way, I’ll steal your food, but then when I’m falling asleep, somebody else will come along and steal my throat. As Hobbes famously put it, in the absence of morality, we’d be in the state of nature. We’d be in the war of all against all. Now let’s see if I can get the quote right: “Life would be nasty, poor, brutish, solitary and short.” A friend of mine who teaches moral philosophy at Michigan said, “If life’s gonna be nasty, poor, solitary, and brutish, being short isn’t so bad." But Hobbes’s thought was, This is what morality is about, the social contract. Hobbes is a kind of contractarian, at least in the interpretation I accept. Basically, we all strike a deal: I agree not to slit your throat in exchange for your agreeing not to slit my throat. Autonomy is not crucial there. What’s crucial there is our finitude, the fact that any one person can be killed by enough other people. Nobody’s Superman; nobody can do it by themselves. That’s a quite different story from the Kantian story about what ethics is all about. As it happens, I’m more sympathetic to the Kantian story. Brooks: Now I’m gonna ask you a few questions that people like me always ask people like you. I’m sure you’ve heard them a zillion times, but I’m just curious what you would say. The first is: Why is rape worse than a punch in the nose? To me, a rape is worse than a punch in the nose because a person contains a soul, and rape is an insult to the soul in a way that the punch in the nose is not. Kagan: I agree, rape seems like an especially horrific thought. To make it even easier: Why is rape a horrible thing to happen to you in a way that your backache is not? The backache could be a more intense pain, but it wouldn’t normally be nearly as psychologically overwhelming, because rape is a direct attack on your autonomy, on your ability to decide for yourself, in central ways, how you want your life to go. Your sexual decisions are among the most central decisions. Rape overrides that in an especially horrific way. Another thing that I think is similar in that way is torture. Torture is deliberately trying to break the person as opposed to merely trying to cause them pain. Certain truths that are central to organizing our worldview shouldn’t be beaten out of us. I believe all of that, but I don’t see why one needs to bring in a soul. When I torture you, or if I were to rape you—there are probably other things of a similar sort—what I would be doing in the most fundamental way is undermining your ability to choose for yourself how your life wants to go. That’s where the autonomy comes in. So the question just gets pushed off. To get ethics going in the way I want it to get going, we need a story about how you can have a creature that is able to set its own goals, to step back. Lots and lots of animals have pretty accurate beliefs about their environment. They make reasonable decisions about how to satisfy their desires in light of the immediate environment. What seems special about us—maybe not unique about us, but certainly special about us—is that we can step back from that. We can say, Yes, I want this. Does it make sense to want that? Yes, doing this would satisfy that desire. Does it make sense to satisfy it in that way or not? That’s where rationality comes in, and rationality and autonomy are tightly connected. So the question becomes: Do you need to believe in anything immaterial in order to believe in this kind of ability? If we were having this conversation 100 years ago or even 50 years ago or maybe even 20 years ago and asked, “Could we really have machines that could reason?,” we’d say, “I don’t know. The jury’s out.” I don’t think the jury’s yet quite come back. But I think it becomes more and more credible to think a physical object is probably capable of reasoning. Brooks: I’m going to try another reason why the concept of a soul appeals to me, aside from my experience of it. My view is that we’re not equal in our level of brain power, and we’re not equal in our level of muscle power. But we are all equal on the level of the soul. We all have the soul of infinite and equal dignity. To me, that’s the basis of human equality. Kagan: I do think it’s an interesting question. If you’ve got a story about the ultimate basis of having moral standing—my own view is that animals count, but they don’t count as much as people do. I owe anybody who’s gonna be on my side a story about what is it that gives you standing that can come in varying degrees. As you say, it’s going then to be an interesting question: Will people differ in that regard? Because if they do, then they maybe will also have different strength rights, or something like that. Suppose you accepted the Hobbesian story. Then it doesn’t matter that you’re stronger than me because I can get three other people and together we can beat you up. You still have to fall asleep. Hobbes, perfectly cognizant of this point, talked about—another piece of jargon—a kind of practical or rough equality. For all practical purposes, any one of us needs the moral contract and so will hold out. It doesn’t matter that you’re smarter than I am, or it doesn’t matter that you’re stronger than I am, or it doesn’t matter that you’re more creative than I am, or whatever it might be—or that I’m needier than you are. I’m not going to agree to avoid killing you and taking your food unless you agree to give me the same rights that you have. Hobbesians have one kind answer. Kant thinks about it in terms of autonomy, and then one might wonder: Are we all equally autonomous? I suspect not. Brooks: Not even close. Kagan: No, not even close. Anybody who’s a deontologist and thinks that it’s ultimately based on autonomy needs to recognize that animals also have autonomy to varying degrees. So maybe they have weaker rights than we have. So you’re going to bring in a soul. You believe in souls. So one question would be: By virtue of what is it true that souls are a plausible story about why we count morally? Second, even if you could tell me a story about that, do souls come in degrees? I take it as a part of the assumption that they don’t. Is that true? St. Francis of Assisi famously preaches to the birds because he believes animals have souls. I haven’t read enough about him to know: Did he think that the birds had souls of a grade-A type? Or did they have grade-B souls? Once you start allowing souls, then maybe all humans have grade-A souls, but maybe you’ve got an A-minus soul, but St. Francis of Assisi had an A-plus soul. Tell me, do you think that souls come in only one-size-fits-all? Brooks: Yes, absolutely. Kagan: Based on what? Brooks: Based on the idea that it would be horrific to think that I was superior to the homeless guy on the street. That would be a morally reprehensible belief. If that’s a morally reprehensible belief, then it must be we all have some level that’s equal, and I think it’s our spiritual natures. Kagan: That’s not bad. Some people would say that’s an illegitimate argument, where you want it to be the case that we all count morally, so you’re going to believe whatever it is that you need metaphysically speaking in order to get that to fall out. I’m not hostile to that kind of argument. Famously, Kant also argues this way. Kant thinks you can argue from moral conclusions to belief in a soul, belief in an afterlife, belief in a God, belief in reward and punishment. It’s loaded—How much does one need to assume in order to get the ethical? Hobbes, as I suggested a moment ago, thinks you don’t need to believe in the soul at all. There might be other ways that you could get that conclusion. If you set yourself the goal of designing a moral system, one thing you need to take into account is: What are people like? And: Are people very good at sussing out micro differences in intelligence or degrees of autonomy or what have you? I think from the point of view of designing moral rules, were I God giving rules to all of mankind, I would think there’s gonna be limits to people’s abilities to understand very complicated rules—rules with too many exception clauses or too many subclauses, or rules that the left-handed people get to do this. There’ll be a kind of pressure to have the rules be similar for everybody. And that might give us equal rights without needing to bring in souls. Brooks: Let me ask you the grandfather of all questions that people like me ask people like you, which is: How did consciousness arise in the brain? Kagan: When people like you ask people like me , I say that’s not my area of philosophy. There’s a whole subarea of philosophy called philosophy of mind. One of the big debates in philosophy of mind is: How do you explain consciousness? Immediately, I’m gonna ask: What do you mean by consciousness ? Because people, even philosophers, will use this term for different things. Let me draw two broad categories of things. Sometimes what ordinary people mean by consciousness is having thoughts, beliefs, desires—putting these things together to make plans and so consequently having intentions. Your thermostat can turn the furnace on and off when it’s warm or cold, but it’s not conscious. It doesn’t have thoughts. It doesn’t have beliefs. If that’s what you mean by consciousness , the question becomes: Can we tell a story about how a physical object can have beliefs, have desires? I think we’ve got the beginnings of a pretty good story, because we can already build machines that can represent environments. To take the trivial example, because it’s as complicated as I get, a chess-playing computer. When you’re playing that program on your computer, it represents the chessboard in a certain way. So it has what I’m perfectly content to say are beliefs about where your bishop is—and does it threaten or does it not threaten its king?—and so forth. Brooks: That strikes me as a very weird definition of consciousness . We program certain algorithms into it, or in AI we’ve programmed the ability to predict the next words or whatever it is. Kagan: No, I’m not sure that the ability to predict the next word counts as that. What I had in mind with the chess-playing computer was that, when it moves its queen to take my bishop, I find it perfectly natural to say something like, “It wanted to capture my bishops because it wants to protect its king from being checked.” Now I find that perfectly congenial, and all I wanted to say was if that’s what you mean by consciousness —having beliefs, having desires, being able to report what those beliefs and desires are, being able to make plans on the basis of them—we already can do that in some rudimentary ways, and we’re getting better and better at it. You say, “That’s not what I mean by consciousness .” I say: “Fine. Here’s the second thing people mean by consciousness . This one is harder to describe, though I imagine everybody’s gonna be familiar with it.” You punch me, and I feel pain. There’ll be various behaviors that I’ll engage in. But there’s something about the experience of pain that we have not yet captured, and maybe that’s what we mean by consciousness . And it’s not limited to the ability to feel pleasure and pain. Right now on the desk, you’ve got a copy of my book. My eyes happen to be going to little red strip on it. So there’s something happening in my mind right now, the experience of red. I take it that when you look at the book—and hold it up so that people rush off to the bookstore to buy a copy of it—you and they will also have something going on inside the experience of red. So sometimes we, or philosophers, mean that inner aspect, by consciousness . Then the question, and I think it’s a great question, is: How do we explain consciousness from a physical point of view? If physicalism is the view that all I am, all you are, is just a physical material object, how do you explain this ability to have this inner aspect of experience? Can a physical object have that? And if so, how do we explain the origins of that? Now the answer is: I don’t know. I think that is the pressing question for physicalists to answer. There are physicalists, there are philosophers who have pet theories about this. I don’t myself. Although it’s not an area of expertise, I don’t find any of them especially attractive. But I don’t think bringing in the soul helps. Suppose you say—I mean, I’m not giving you a chance to say—but suppose you say, “Ah, this is why I believe in a soul; posit a soul, and now we can explain how it can happen.” I say, “You haven’t explained anything. You’ve just said, ‘Imagine there’s a thing that somehow can generate consciousness. I don’t know how it can do it.’” You don’t have a theory, and I don’t have a theory. So that doesn’t give us any special reason to start positing souls. Brooks: I would put it a little differently. I would say we have three pounds of meat in our brain, and we produce ecstasy. We produce “Ode to Joy.” I’m realizing that one of our distinctions is you’re a physicalist, I’m a spookiest. I think the world is spooky. So it doesn’t really surprise me that meat could produce consciousness. But for you, if you think meat is all there is, then the fact that you can’t explain the fundamental human experience, which is subjective experience, is kind of a problem for your worldview. Kagan: Well, it is a problem in the sense that it’s an unsolved problem. First of all, I think the world is spooky and strange and weird too. Philosophers are basically people who never got over the thought that, Boy, the world’s a really weird place, and I don’t understand very much of it . Aristotle famously said, “Philosophy begins in wonder." And I just wanna say that it continues in complete bafflement. Brooks: I can’t help pointing out that Descartes said that wonder is a surprise of the soul, so I’ll just add that. Kagan: Again, I’m not unhappy using soul talk. When you start saying, “And by a soul , I mean to be stipulating something nonphysical,” then I say, “Why is that the best hypothesis as to all this cool stuff, all this weird ability to fall in love and to write poetry and to feel ecstasy?” I think we can offer certain explanations for creativity from a physicalist point of view. I don’t think we can yet do it for consciousness. But does this trouble me? Well, I take some comfort in the thought that we’re just beginning to do brain science. To say we’re in the Middle Ages is too generous. We’re in the dawn of time in terms of brain science. So the analogy I always give in my death class is: 100 years ago, 150 years ago, 300 years ago, 500 years ago, if you asked people how to explain life, the answer would’ve been: We haven’t a clue how you could explain life in physical terms. It must be that there’s something nonphysical going on there. And the answer was: Come back in 300 years, 500 years, 700 years. It turns out now we have an explanation. We don’t know all the details, but we know enough to know we can offer. My money—it’s nothing more than that—but I conjecture, come back in 300 years, 700 years, we’ll have a story as to how consciousness could emerge from three pounds of meat. Brooks: You could answer any argument with that, though. Kagan: Look, I’ll concede, I do concede. I make a point of emphasizing this. I don’t think we have a story yet. But the question is: To believe in a soul, you’ve gotta think it’s got the upper hand somewhere, and I would agree with that if you could give me even the outlines of a story. How is an immaterial thing going to experience an inner life? Brooks: Let me read a sentence from your book, which I disagreed with. Kagan: Great. Brooks: You write, “Try introspecting for a moment. Turn your mind’s eye inward and ask, ‘Do you see a soul inside you?’ I don’t think you will. Like me, you may observe various sensations in your body. You may observe various thoughts and feelings, but you won’t observe a soul." Now, I do. When I wake up in the morning, or I’m in the middle of my day, sometimes my soul is soaring, and sometimes my soul is degraded. The Psalmist famously says, “Why are you downcast, O my soul?" The way I experience my soul mostly is in yearning. Yearning for self-transcendence. Yearning to expand outside myself. The stuff I pour into my soul, the different experiences, have different effects on it. Furthermore, what I’m describing is not uncommon. Kagan: Of course. Brooks: I actually looked up all these words in different cultures for soul. You know the one in Hebrew, it’s nephesh; Egyptian, ka ; Chinese, hun ; Arabic, nafs ; Ghana, okra . All these different cultures all around the world independently have a central concept in all their cultures: Humans have souls. And it’s a spiritual, immaterial thing. Why are all these cultures wrong? Kagan: They don’t all have the immaterial thing. They have a word that we can translate as soul . Then the question is: What does the word soul mean in English ,and are we translating it properly or not? Dualism—the view that there is this immaterial thing in addition to the body—is a philosophical conjecture that some people believe and other people don’t believe, and some religious traditions teach and other religious traditions don’t teach. Even Christianity hasn’t always been dualist. The early Christians believed in part in bodily resurrection because there was no way to be around after your death without your body because they didn’t believe in souls. And then Plato comes along— Brooks: But they would say the spirit infused every piece of them. It wasn’t separate. Kagan: You gave a number of moving sentences a minute or two minutes ago, before I interrupted. I wish I had a transcript of those sentences. When you say, “My soul soars,” if I’d gone through, and any place you said soul, I just said, “ I soar, I’m ecstatic, I’m moved, I’m down in the dumps,” I’m not sure what we would’ve lost. Now, there’s a use of the word soul in English, as in lots of other cultures, where it’s a way of talking about the fact that when you listen to Mozart or I listen to Dylan, something is happening to me that is not happening to me, I will confess, when I listen to Lady Gaga. Something happens to me. I am moved by that. Fine, I believe in all of that, and I’m not remotely troubled in saying I want to reserve the word soul , or at least I want to use the word soul , in those contexts. If we wanted to talk about our essence—the deepest, most central parts about our beliefs, our desires, our values, the memories that are most cherished—and you want to say “sacred,” I have no problems with that kind of language at all. I think soul is a useful word for characterizing those aspects, those elements, those components. If we use the word personality for all of your beliefs, all of your memories, all of your goals, all of your desires, and then soul for that central subset that you would feel like you had died if you had to give those things up, I’m perfectly happy with that. The mistake is to think that if we are gonna talk that way, you must be positing something nonphysical. Brooks: Let me describe to you what I think a soul is, because I think we probably have a little overlap. So I have a hobby. Well, it’s my job. But I interview neuroscientists, because I’m just interested in what they’re doing. When I started doing this, 25 years ago, they were super interested in where things were happening in the brain. You’d go to conferences, and there’d be some BS corporate consultant, and he would say, “This shows the amygdala’s lighting up, and therefore, that shows blah, blah, blah,” and it was all nonsense. But now they don’t think that way. They talk about these vast neural coalitions that cross a lot of different regions. There’s a neuroscientist, I wanna give him credit, Luiz Pessoa, who compares these networks, these vast, widely distributed networks. He calls them neuronal ensembles distributed across multiple brain regions, and he compares them to a murmuring of swallows. My intuition, though I don’t know, is that consciousness emerges from that murmuration. But I would say, also, the soul emerges from that. So it’s not without physical basis. We’re infused. But the soul emerges from the swirl. The soul is the swirl. And emergent properties, as you know very well—you take a bunch of physical things, and out of their interaction, a new quality emerges. Some people have a low version of emergent that you can understand that high quality by looking at the physical low qualities. Other people have a strong version of emergence, which is you can’t understand the high quality. It takes on independent conditions that are its own thing, and then it has a downward pressure on everything underneath. I take a strong emergent view. All of that swirl, all that energy state, creates this new thing. The quality of our soul then influences how we feel, how we act, how we do, what we want. Kagan: So maybe you really are a physicalist as well. It’s just that you think that you want to save the word soul , and you want to think about soul as this thing that emerges at the global level, which is fine. I’m perfectly happy to think about consciousness as something that emerges at the global level. You put enough neurons together the right way, and we’ll get either consciousness or something like that. Okay, great. I’m even happy—maybe, depending on how much you mean—in thinking that there’ll be things where the fundamental explanation needs to be done at the global level, not at the micro level. But you don’t have to pretend that physicalism isn’t true. Or you shouldn’t persuade yourself, would be a better way to put it, that physicalism isn’t true to believe in this kind of emergent stuff at the global level. Brooks: I’m trying to give some reasons why I think there’s a soul. But there’s a set of experiences I’ve had that are not reasonable. I’ll tell you one story. I was in New York, like, 11 years ago. In New York City, a city I love, the ugliest spot on the face of the Earth—used to be … it’s still pretty ugly—is Penn Station, the train station. There’s only one possibly uglier spot, which is the subway station next to Penn Station. So I’m there on whatever Eighth Avenue line, and I look around the car one morning, and I get the sensation that everybody in this car has souls. My sensation is these souls, in each case, are in movement. Some are going up and some are going down, degraded. Thomas Aquinas talks about all these movements. And then I thought, Well, I feel this . That is not the only (what they call) “numinous” experience that I’ve had. In nature, with my kids, whatever. When I have those experiences, the arguments almost don’t matter. Kagan: I’m glad you brought this up again because this allows me to do something I meant to do several minutes ago, when you quoted the sentence about peering inside and not seeing soul. This is a point I just learned from David Hume, another British philosopher. When he peers inside, he can sense experiences, pleasures, pains, thoughts, wishes, hopes, desires. He doesn’t experience any soul. Putting words into his mouth, that’s a philosophical conjecture as to how these things can occur. So I just wanna say, yeah, you were in this moment, and I’ve had similar moments as well. You’re just taken by the magnificence of humanity, the fact that every one of us is a unique individual and has the things that we’re trying to do, and some of us are getting there, and some of us are not getting there, and some of us are on the wrong path, but hopefully we’ll make and others never will. We can have all these thoughts. Having these thoughts is important. Again, I’m not any kind of foe of spiritual talk. If you find it most comfortable to express these thoughts in spiritual language, I won’t deny you them. It’s only when you start doing metaphysics— Brooks: So we have a metaphysical difference. But I guess one of my questions is: What difference does it make? We have totally different viewpoints on this, but how do our different viewpoints affect our lives and how we should live our lives? It sounds like you’re saying it almost makes no difference. I’ve invented some word soul , which you think doesn’t exist. But do you think it affects lives when you shift from being a physicalist to a spookiest? Kagan: It needn’t, in the same way that it needn’t when you go from being a spookiest to being a physicalist. I’m afraid I no longer remember, but I conjecture that when I was young, I believed in something nonphysical. And it was through doing philosophy I came to see that, as far as I could see, one could continue to espouse the things that were important to me about, call it, the spiritual side of life, without buying into a bunch of metaphysical baggage that I no longer find myself inclined to think was the most plausible metaphysics. Didn’t have to give it up. Now for some people, giving up religion just is part and parcel of a transformation in which they give up not just the spiritual, but they give up the moral, and they give up the ethics. I’ve had any number of discussions with religious figures who basically look at me and say, “How can you have morality without God or a soul?” Hobbes has a story about how you could have it. And I think Kant has a story about how you could have it.. There’s no logical reason—if you want to believe in right and wrong and equality and human dignity—that you’ll have an easier time of it if you believe that there’s this nonmaterial object that maybe continues to exist after our biological organism decays. I don’t think that extra bit of metaphysics gets you anywhere closer to the ethics stuff and the value stuff and the spiritual stuff that you and I are in agreement is important. Brooks: Well, Shelly Kagan, it’s such a pleasure to talk with you. Kagan: It’s been a pleasure. Thank you very much. Brooks: Thanks for joining my conversation with Shelly Kagan. As you could tell, we probably disagree pretty drastically on some of the biggest issues of life. But what I love about Shelly is that even though he doesn’t believe there’s a soul, he doesn’t believe there’s a purpose to the universe, he doesn’t believe there’s an afterlife, that has not made him a cold and technical and overly rational person. He’s a deeply moral person. He’s a deeply warm person. I don’t know if Shelly would like me saying this, but you could even describe him as soulful. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener . See you next week.

items.title: Bahass Foundation launches vocational skills training to support mental health recovery in Wa
items.description: The Bahass Foundation has marked this year’s World Mental Health Day with the launch of a vocational skills training initiative aimed at empowering residents undergoing rehabilitation and reducing relapses linked to unemployment and social stigma. The initiative provides practical training in tailoring, smock dressmaking and traditional weaving to help residents acquire skills they can use to earn a living and reintegrate into their communities after rehabilitation. The Chief Executive Officer of the Bahass Foundation, Ilyasu Yussif Baba, said clinical rehabilitation alone was insufficient if beneficiaries returned to environments where they lacked productive activities and sustainable livelihoods. “Rehabilitation alone cannot solve all problems. Many of them, when they go back, do not have anything doing. That is why we decided to launch skills training, so when they are out, they have something productive to rely on rather than sitting idle,” Mr Baba explained. According to Mr Baba, substance abuse accounts for approximately 80 per cent of current admissions at the facility, while other cases are associated with acute financial stress, business collapse or marital breakdown. The facility currently houses 72 residents, comprising 60 males and 12 females. At the time of the event, 18 residents had started the vocational training, with two already able to produce woven items independently. The potential impact of the initiative was evident among the residents. Gifty Mary Sunchebe, a resident from Nandom who developed a substance abuse problem while living in Koforidua, demonstrated how she coils thread for smock weaving. “Coming here has given me a new skill. When I go home, I will show my parents what I can do so they can support me to start on my own,” she said. She also urged families not to abandon relatives struggling with substance dependence. Another resident, Bayuo Fortunatus, who is learning smock weaving, said vocational skills could help people recovering from mental health conditions overcome social stigma and achieve financial independence. “Being in a mental home does not mean your life has ended. Employment issues affect everyone. Once you acquire a viable skill, you go out into the world able to provide for yourself and stay stable,” Fortunatus noted. The event also featured a testimony of successful community reintegration by Mohammed, popularly known as “Killer Ntua”, a former resident who recovered at the facility, married and returned with his wife, Latifa, and young son, Abdul Rashid, to express gratitude to the foundation. Ali Labaran, a resident undergoing rehabilitation, highlighted the facility’s dual role as a recovery centre and an addiction detoxification facility. “Addiction, if left unchecked, will eventually drive a person into acute mental illness. We chose to be here with the backing of our families to reclaim our futures,” Labaran said. Addressing the gathering, the Upper West Regional Mental Health Coordinator, Sylvester Basagnia, commended the foundation for placing the experiences and perspectives of people with lived experience at the centre of its activities. However, he warned against the widespread stigma, derogatory labelling and abandonment of people experiencing mental health challenges by their families and communities. “The fact that someone has schizophrenia, depression or an addiction does not mean their name has changed to that illness. Address people with dignity by their real names,” Mr Basagnia urged. He cited the case of a trained senior high school teacher in Wa whose employment was terminated and payroll records erased after he developed mental health complications, leaving him destitute on the streets. Mr Basagnia also raised concerns about substance abuse in the Wa Municipality, particularly the use of tramadol, pethidine, illicit alcohol and smokeless powdered snuff, locally known as nyee. The chairman for the occasion, Biihee Naa, Naa Jaafar Pelpuo, emphasised that mental health challenges could affect anyone, regardless of social status or religious devotion. “Mental illness is a common affliction that spares no one. If you find yourself in sound health, do not assume you are merely favoured while those afflicted are cursed. Supporting them to heal is supporting our own community’s wellbeing,” Naa Pelpuo stated. The Coordinator of the Wa Community Foundation, Fatawu Dauda, described Bahass as an indispensable pillar in the Upper West Region, providing food, shelter and dignity to people living on the streets when their families are unable to care for them. The event also attracted donations from community organisations in support of the foundation’s work. The Jawara Foundation, led by its National Coordinator, Francis Baaladong, donated clothing, bags of rice, cooking oil, detergents, toiletries and GH₵1,000 in cash. The Cathedral Parish branch of the Society of St. Theresa of the Child Jesus, represented by Diana Ali, donated clothing, toiletries and GH₵500 in cash. The Upper West branch of Muslim Women in Teaching (MUSWIT), led by its patron, Sahadatu Y. Dodoo, also made financial donations and urged families to listen to relatives experiencing distress before their conditions worsened. Despite its achievements, including the successful rehabilitation of more than 48 individuals, the Bahass Foundation faces significant infrastructural challenges. All 72 residents are currently accommodated in a single compound house. Mr Baba appealed to philanthropic organisations, government agencies and the general public to provide building materials and financial assistance to complete an ongoing dormitory project, which has stalled at the window stage.

items.title: Développement communal : Le maire du Golfe 6 renforce le dialogue avec les leaders religieux musulmans
items.description: Lomé, 10 oct. (ATOP) – Le maire du Golfe 6, Kokou Amenyenou a échangé, le vendredi 9 octobre, avec des responsables religieuses musulmans sur leur implication dans la gestion participative des affaires de la commune et la cohésion pacifique avec les autres communautés. Les imams des mosquées et autres leaders religieux musulmans et prédicateurs de la commune Golfe 6 ont pris part à cette séance d’échanges avec le conseil municipal. Elle s’inscrit dans la volonté de la municipalité de renforcer la concertation avec les différentes composantes de la société. La présente séance fait suite à deux précédentes rencontres qui ont réuni d’abord le conseil municipal et les pasteurs, et d’autre part les prêtres catholiques et traditionnels. Les échanges ont porté essentiellement sur le civisme, les différents frais à payer, l’éducation, l’état civil, la salubrité et la cohésion sociale, de même que le rôle important des leaders religieux dans la sensibilisation des fidèles, en raison de leur proximité avec les familles, les jeunes et les différents groupes sociaux. L’importance des déclarations régulières de naissance et de l’obtention de documents authentiques, indispensables à la reconnaissance de l’identité et à l’accès aux droits. La question relative à la lenteur administrative dans le traitement des dossiers de délivrance de la nationalité a retenu l’attention des participants. La problématique de la naturalisation des étrangers ayant épousé des femmes togolaises ou ayant des enfants nés des femmes togolaises a été aussi abordée. Les personnes concernées ont été orientées vers le ministère de le Justice et des Droits humains. La réduction des nuisances sonores et le respect de la tranquillité publique ont été également au centre des discussions, ceci pour favoriser une cohabitation harmonieuse entre les différentes communautés. Par rapport aux inquiétudes relatives aux différents frais, La municipalité a fait savoir que celles-ci trouveront des solutions après le vote du prochain budget. Les leaders religieux ont été appelés à sensibiliser les fidèles sur les conséquences des actes frauduleux et à les orienter vers les procédures légales auprès des services compétents. L’exécutif communal a, par ailleurs, invité ses interlocuteurs à renforcer les messages de paix, de tolérance, de respect mutuel et de vivre-ensemble. Ils ont été invités à promouvoir le civisme, le respect des règles de vie en société et la responsabilité citoyenne au sein de leurs communautés. Le maire Amenyenou, a annoncé que la commune envisage de mettre en place un cadre permanent de dialogue avec les responsables religieux et les organisations locales. Ce mécanisme, a-t-il déclaré, devrait favoriser le partage régulier des préoccupations des populations, la coordination des actions de sensibilisation et la recherche de réponses collectives aux défis de la commune. Le président de l’Union musulmane du Togo, section Baguida, Imam Ali Sossah, a invité ses coreligionnaires à une cohabitation pacifique dans la pratique quotidienne de leur religion. Il a évoqué notamment la question de nuisance sonore, qui constitue souvent une gêne pour leurs voisins immédiats ou lointains. ATOP/KYA/BV

items.title: El Papa anuncia que tiene un nódulo en un pulmón y va a ser operado
items.description: El papa León XIV, de 71 años, ha anunciado por sorpresa este domingo, tras el rezo del Ángelus desde la ventana de su apartamento en el Vaticano, que tiene un nódulo en un pulmón y va a ser operado en los próximos días. “Los médicos han encontrado un nódulo circunscrito al pulmón. Se ha detectado en una fase muy temprana y bien localizado. Los médicos consideran oportuno intervenir, por lo que, siguiendo su consejo, he decidido someterme a una operación para extirparlo. El procedimiento ya está programado para los próximos días. Les agradezco su cercanía espiritual y me encomiendo a sus oraciones”, ha dicho a los fieles. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Centrafrique: les mariages précoces toujours d’actualité, en cette Journée internationale des filles
items.description: Le monde célèbre, ce dimanche 11 octobre, la Journée internationale de la fille. Instaurée en 2012 par l’ONU, elle vise à faire reconnaître les difficultés particulières auxquelles les filles et les adolescentes sont confrontées. En Centrafrique, le mariage forcé ou précoce demeure une réalité pour de nombreuses jeunes filles, parfois au nom des traditions, des coutumes ou de la religion. Pourtant, la loi interdit cette pratique.

items.title: Cancer du sein : Mathilde Panot dénonce les liens entre l’initiateur d’Octobre rose et Israël
items.description: La députée de La France insoumise (LFI) Mathilde Panot est accusée par Marine Le Pen d'antisémitisme pour avoir refusé de prendre part à la campagne « Octobre rose » de dépistage du cancer du sein . La parlementaire de gauche maintient sa position et ses révélations sur les pratiques extrêmement graves d’une multinationale de pesticides et de sa filiale israélienne. Panot a refusé de porter un ruban rose à l’Assemblée nationale, dans le cadre d'une campagne de soutien à la lutte contre le cancer du sein. « La lutte contre le cancer ne doit pas être du vernis rose. Nous ne voulons pas un Octobre rose, mais un Octobre colère », affirme-t-elle, révélant que c'est une multinationale de pesticides qui est à l'origine de la campagne « Octobre rose » pour élargir son marché. Les pratiques « criminelles » d’une multinationale et de sa filiale israélienne La présidente du groupe parlementaire LFI a de sérieuses raisons de ne pas se joindre à la campagne. Elle les a expliquées dans une vidéo partagée sur les réseaux sociaux. « Quand on gratte le vernis rose, on découvre le cynisme absolu », dit-elle. La multinationale en question, c'est Syngenta, le plus gros producteur de pesticides au monde, et contre laquelle, rappelle Mathilde Panot, 15 000 personnes ont manifesté ce week-end en France, car elle « répand la mort partout dans le monde ». Syngenta, poursuit l’élue de gauche, c'est aussi sa filiale israélienne Adama qui produit des pesticides génériques. « Syngenta est donc étroitement liée au projet d’expansion coloniale d’Israël, qui répand massivement des pesticides pour détruire les terres palestiniennes et libanaises », accuse-t-elle. Une multinationale de pesticides à l'origine d'« Octobre rose » ? Et ce n'est pas tout. Panot rappelle que Syngenta s'appelait l’Imperial Chemical Industries, qui « fabriquait notamment des pesticides comme le DDT, un perturbateur endocrinien et cancérigène », et commercialisait aussi « un traitement contre le cancer du sein ». « Ils vendent le poison qui vous rend malade et ils vendent ensuite le traitement pour cette même maladie, voilà comment les empoisonneurs font double profit », dénonce la députée. Au milieu des années 1980, poursuit-elle dans ses révélations, la même multinationale, trouvant son marché du cancer du sein « trop restreint », a eu l’idée, « pour l’élargir et favoriser le dépistage », de lancer la campagne devenue Octobre rose en France. C'est d'ailleurs l'origine du terme « pinkwashing », qui est le fait d'utiliser la santé comme campagne de marketing ou « pour justifier les horreurs ». « Le cancer est une maladie politique » C’est, selon Mathilde Panot, ce qui se passe ce mois-ci à l’Assemblée nationale où, accuse-t-elle, « la Macronie, la droite et l’extrême-droite s'épinglent la poitrine de rose quelques semaines après avoir forcé la réintroduction de pesticides qui s'attaquent directement au cerveau des enfants ». « Le Rassemblement national a voté contre la prise en charge totale des traitements du cancer du sein par l'assurance maladie. Ces gens sont des hypocrites », s’écrie-t-elle. « Le cancer est une maladie politique donc issue de choix politiques », conclut la députée LFI. Ruban rose : que signifie-t-il et pourquoi je ne le porterai pas durant ce mois d'octobre ? La lutte contre le cancer ne doit pas être du vernis rose. Nous ne voulons pas un « Octobre rose », mais un Octobre colère. Explications https://t.co/zTz9znIfx4 — Mathilde Panot (@MathildePanot) October 9, 2026 L’article Cancer du sein : Mathilde Panot dénonce les liens entre l’initiateur d’Octobre rose et Israël est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Miss Littérature Sénégal : dix candidates en lice pour la finale du 14 novembre
items.description: La deuxième édition de Miss Littérature Sénégal connaît ses dix finalistes. À l’issue de la demi-finale organisée le samedi 10 octobre 2026, au Complexe culturel Léopold Sédar Senghor de Pikine, dix candidates ont décroché leur ticket pour la grande finale, prévue le 14 novembre prochain à l’Institut français de Dakar. La compétition entre dans sa dernière ligne droite. Lancée pour promouvoir le livre, la lecture et l’excellence intellectuelle féminine, Miss Littérature Sénégal entend également mettre en lumière les jeunes talents littéraires du pays. Elles étaient en lice pour franchir cette étape décisive. Au terme de la demi-finale, dix candidates ont été retenues pour poursuivre l’aventure. Il s’agit de Khadidiatou Kane, Fatou Binetou Sène, Aïcha Rose Niassy, Mame Mbayame Niang, Dieynaba Bâ, Niama Boumaré, Aïda Bâ, Sophie Charlene Nasala, Fatoumata Diagne et Ndeye Ndiaye. La finale, prévue le 14 novembre 2026 à l’Institut français de Dakar, constituera la dernière étape de cette deuxième édition. Les candidates auront l’occasion d’y défendre leur parcours et leur engagement en faveur de la littérature. À travers cette initiative, le comité d’organisation, dirigé par Salamata Ousmane Diallo, réaffirme son ambition de faire de la lecture et de la culture des leviers d’épanouissement et de valorisation du potentiel intellectuel féminin. Au-delà du concours, Miss Littérature Sénégal entend contribuer au rayonnement de la littérature sénégalaise et encourager les jeunes femmes à investir davantage l’univers du livre. A.N

items.title: ‎Initiative presidentielle pour la relève et la promotion de l’élite sportive : L’Ambassadeur pour le sport joue la carte de la Ligue de l’Espoir (LIDE)
items.description: Le stade Wobi de Bobo-Dioulasso a abrité samedi 10 octobre, le lancement officiel de la première édition de la Ligue de l’Espoir (LIDE). Portée par l'Ambassadeur pour le Sport, le Camarade Charles KABORÉ, ancien capitaine des Étalons, cette compétition, réservée aux moins de 17 ans (U17), s’inscrit dans la vision du Chef de l’État, le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ, à travers l’Initiative Présidentielle pour la Relève et la Promotion de l’Élite Sportive. Le Ministre Secrétaire Général du Gouvernement, le Camarade Ousmane OUATTARA, représentant le Premier ministre, Patron de cette édition, a, dans son discours, relevé le rôle cardinal de la jeunesse dans la Révolution Progressiste Populaire : « Le Chef de l'État, le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ, place la jeunesse au cœur de la transformation nationale (…) Investir dans la jeunesse, c'est préparer l'avenir de la Nation. Structurer le sport à la base, c'est donner à cette jeunesse des fondations solides pour bâtir l'avenir ». Selon l'Ambassadeur pour le Sport, le Camarade Charles KABORÉ, ce championnat représente une opportunité majeure d'expression et de visibilité pour les jeunes de 13 à 17 ans. « C’est une initiative très importante pour la jeunesse sportive et la promotion de nos compétences (…) Cette compétition offre une opportunité aux jeunes d’être détectés par de grands clubs nationaux et étrangers », a-t-il souligné. Au-delà des aspects compétitifs, avec ce projet ambitieux et s'appuyant sur son expérience, il s'agit pour l'ancien capitaine des Étalons, de transmettre les exigences du milieu professionnel aux plus jeunes. « On veut créer ce cadre-là pour qu'ils soient régulièrement en compétition, comme nous, on l'a été dans le temps. (…) Aujourd'hui nous venons traduire cette expérience ici avec l'accompagnement du Camarade Président, Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ », a expliqué l’Ambassadeur pour le Sport. Cette édition de la LIDE réunit 16 formations réparties entre Bobo-Dioulasso et Ouagadougou, et pose les bases d’un renouveau du football national. Elle ambitionne de devenir un pilier durable du développement du football burkinabè. C'est une initiative qui est mise en œuvre en attendant la Ligue de la Souveraineté, annoncée à l'issue du Conseil des ministres du jeudi dernier avec une plus large ouverture en termes de catégories et une envergure nationale prenant en compte toutes les régions du pays. Le match inaugural de cette première édition de la Ligue de l’Espoir a vu la victoire des U17 de Rahimo FC sur ceux de Vitesse FC par 3 buts à 2. ‎Direction de la communication de la Présidence du Faso

items.title: La consommation de la grenade est bonne pour le cœur
items.description: La production tunisienne de grenades pour la saison 2026 est estimée à 98 000 tonnes, en hausse de 8 % par rapport aux 91 000 tonnes récoltées en 2025, selon les données du Groupement interprofessionnel des fruits (GIFruits). Ç a tombe bien, puisque, selon Dr Faouzi Addad, la consommation de ce fruit qui mûrit en pareille saison de l’année est excellente pour la santé et pourrait même contribuer à diminuer la pression artérielle. «S’il y a un fruit à mettre à l’honneur durant cette période, c’est bien la grenade (dite la pomme de Carthage). Ses petits grains rouges renferment des fibres et une remarquable diversité de polyphénols, notamment des anthocyanes. La grenade contient également des punicalagines, des composés étudiés pour leurs propriétés antioxydantes et anti-inflammatoires» , écrit le professeur en cardiologie dans un post sur sa page Facebook, où il conseille la consommation de la grenade, de préférence sous forme de jus. Pourquoi la grenade intéresse-t-elle les cardiologues ? Réponse du Pr Addad dans le même post: «Plusieurs études suggèrent des effets favorables sur certains marqueurs du stress oxydatif et de l’inflammation, deux mécanismes impliqués dans les maladies cardiovasculaires et dans la rigidité artérielle.» Il ajoute : «Sa consommation, surtout étudiée sous forme de jus, pourrait aussi contribuer à diminuer la pression artérielle. Les résultats sont encourageants, même s’ils varient beaucoup d’une étude à l’autre.» Bien entendu la consommation de la grenade ne fait disparaître les plaques d’athérosclérose ni ne remplace les traitements. «Son intérêt est de trouver sa place dans une alimentation favorable à notre santé» , précise Pr Addad, qui conseille à ses patients de profiter de la saison pour consommer les grains de grenade,qu’il qualifie de «meilleur alliée pour votre cœur et vos artères» . Il conseille, également, de la consommer «nature et sans sucre ajouté, plutôt que de grands verres de jus (riche en sucre)» , afin de conserver les fibres. «En salade ou avec un yaourt nature, elle apportera couleur, saveur et variété à votre assiette» , conclut-il, comme pour vous mettre de l’eau à l bouche. I. B. L’article La consommation de la grenade est bonne pour le cœur est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Ouagadougou : Un artiste musicien condamné à 60 mois de prison pour tentative cambriolage
items.description: Jugé le lundi 5 octobre 2026 devant la chambre correctionnelle du Tribunal de grande instance de Ouaga I pour une tentative de cambriolage commise dans la nuit du 19 au 20 août dernier, un artiste musicien de 25 ans a été reconnu coupable de tentative de vol. Selon les éléments d'audience rapportés par le média spécialisé Justice Infos Burkina , le prévenu, surpris dans un magasin d'ordinateurs qu'il avait forcé à l'aide d'un marteau, a été condamné à une peine de cinq ans de prison, dont six mois ferme, et à une amende de 500 000 FCFA. Les faits se sont déroulés dans la nuit du 19 au 20 août 2026, aux environs de 2 heures du matin. Profitant de la fermeture des commerces et de l'obscurité, Abdoul (nom d’emprunt), un artiste musicien âgé de 25 ans, a ciblé une boutique de vente de matériel informatique. Pour s'introduire à l'intérieur, le jeune homme a arraché une fenêtre en s'aidant d'un marteau que lui avait remis un ami. À la barre de la chambre correctionnelle du Tribunal de grande instance de Ouaga I, lors de l'audience du lundi 5 octobre 2026, le prévenu a reconnu sans détour l'intégralité des faits qui lui sont reprochés. La tentative d'effraction a cependant été interrompue de façon inattendue. Le commerçant propriétaire des lieux, repassant devant son magasin vers 2 heures du matin, a été intrigué par des bruits suspects à l'intérieur. En vérifiant, il a découvert le prévenu dans le local et a tenté de le maîtriser. Une altercation physique s'est ensuivie, au cours de laquelle Abdoul a sorti un coupe-ongles. Pris de panique face à cet objet, le commerçant s'est enfui en poussant des cris d'alerte, ce qui a immédiatement mobilisé les riverains et permis l'interpellation du suspect. Devant les juges, le prévenu a affirmé avoir sorti cet ustensile uniquement pour se dégager alors que la victime le tenait à la gorge. Comme l'indique la relation des débats publiée par Justice Infos Burkina , le ministère public a estimé la culpabilité du prévenu parfaitement établie au regard des aveux constants faits au commissariat puis devant le parquet. Le procureur avait initialement requis une peine de 60 mois d’emprisonnement, dont 24 mois ferme, assortie d'une amende de 2 000 000 FCFA. Bien que le prévenu ait sollicité la clémence de la cour en plaidant une première infraction et en promettant de ne plus recommencer, le tribunal l'a déclaré coupable. En délibéré contradictoire, les juges l'ont condamné à 60 mois d’emprisonnement, dont six mois ferme , ainsi qu'à une amende ferme de 500 000 FCFA . L’article Ouagadougou : Un artiste musicien condamné à 60 mois de prison pour tentative cambriolage est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .
